subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
That this House, considering the necessity for a reform of our troubled dairy industry, requests that the government immediately introduce its policy on dairy products and, furthermore, that it announce an increase of two dollars in the price paid per hundredweight of milk.
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to speak as member for Joliette, a constituency very much interested in that
March 22, 1974

industry which is experiencing difficulties and danger at the present time. As I must reply first to those who are involved in the dairy industry in my constituency, and considering the importance for the dairy producers in my province who represent, I believe, 50 per cent of the dairy production in this country, and without forgetting of course all the milk producers throughout Canada who are also worried, I am convinced that our party had to reply to the invitation of the people responsible for the dairy farmers of Canada as well as the Quebec Federation, and all those closely or less closely connected to it, to consider such an important question, since the minister responsible for this should also let us know about the decisions of the Canadian Dairy Commission in a few days.
I believe our suggestions, our speeches today will, I hope, reply to the people concerned and to the suggestions they made to us a long time ago and I hope of course the suggestions and recommendations that I will have the opportunity to make and that all members will make to the government will prompt the government to reply in a very clear and precise way, taking account of the importance of this question.
We readily recognize that the milk producers' situation is untenable and again, as I know that the Canadian Dairy Commission will let us know their new policy in a few days, it was exceedingly important, I believe, to select this day and to enable all parties to speak on this question. In this way, we meet fondest wishes of all those concerned with this industry.
Mr. Speaker, the dairy farmers of Quebec and the dairy farmers of Canada who produce industrial or fluid milk met with representatives of all political parties. The members held discussions recently with these officials and we know full well that the officials of the dairy industry are still waiting for the answer they sought. Considering the importance of an early answer, I believe it is our duty to press the government to intervene much more rapidly.
Mr. Speaker, why are we in such a situation and why has the government waited so long? Personally I have been receiving briefs from responsible organizations warning of the danger facing us and this dairy industry today, namely the possible collapse and the obvious inadequacy of milk production in this country.
Responsible organizations have made repeated representations and requests to the government which were ignored, I regret to say. For this reason alone, we are holding today a special debate on the matter and we note a deep concern among milk producers as well as a reduction in the number of milk producers which is increasingly being felt.
Therefore, does the government intend to act? I feel that all the same the government cannot allow such an industry to deteriorate much longer. We are quite aware of the importance of this industry for the consumer or the ordinary citizen, as well as the huge amounts invested in it. Therefore, we have every reason to believe that the government intends to act, but we thought that it was about to act five, four or three years ago.
Once again, this year we find ourselves in a situation where responsible organizations have to send delegates to Ottawa to try and sensitize us again as well as to urge us
Dairy Policy
as an opposition party to force the government into action. I think this is unfortunate. Today I hope that by outlining our party's position which fully agrees with the recommendations of the dairy farmers of Canada, there will be no hesitation. We urge the government to respond to the dairy farmers, that is to meet the producers' wishes and requirements.
Therefore, in view of the fact that my province produces 50 per cent of the Canadian milk, I am calling upon all Quebec members to compel the government to meet the essential requirements which would enable the producers to stay in business.
I would like to make a few remarks on the main recommendations made by the Dairy Farmers of Canada. They make no bones about saying that the government should formally commit itself without delay to implement a national policy providing that it will use our dairy production to meet the needs of Canadians.
It is only natural that milk producers should obtain the assurance that they may produce according to consumer needs. And if a government will not acknowledge this fact, I wonder why, because it would then prevent Canadians from producing a commodity which would meet Canadian needs.
The brief goes on, and I quote:
2.	Never in the past have the representatives of the milk producers of Canada, assembled in annual meeting of Dairy Farmers of Canada felt so strong a sense of urgency and concern: urgency over the need for basic commitments and decisions that must be made by the Government of Canada over the next month or two; concern that if those commitments are not made, and the decisions wisely taken, serious and perhaps irreparable harm will be done to Canada's dairy industry, and to the basic interests of Canadian consumers and the Canadian economy.
3.	There are three essentia] priorities:
(i)	an overall increase in returns to industrial milk and cream
production equivalent to at least $2.00 per hundred pounds of milk.
As all hon. members know, government ministers met with Quebec officials recently. That was reported in the press, and it was shown that an additional $2 would be a minimum. As for us, we understood that those figures were justified and the needs were real, and we readily support that recommendation which is vital for the future of the milk industry.
Is this government now in a position to respond in the same way rather than wait a few more weeks? We know producers are concerned and it is up to us to dispel those anxieties. I think this government could at least answer this question today by making, and I quote:
(ii)	a commitment by the federal government, and preferably by
Parliament in legislative form, to future maintenance of income from
milk production at fully adequate levels.
I said earlier that it is absolutely necessary for us to try and match production with consumption. Of course, it is always difficult for the Commission to come up with accurate forecasts. However, when we consider that this year, we had to import 54 million pounds of butter, we have every reason to be shocked by those irresponsible and inaccurate forecasts. Therefore, milk producers have grounds for complaint, because they are compelled to restrict their production and to accept butter imports worth 54 million pounds.

March 22, 1974
Dairy Policy
It has also been stated in the light of serious studies made that as the situation is now evolving, we will have to import another 100 million pounds of butter. I would think that no one in this House will accept that without a word and that we will all try to force the government into acting quickly.
I was told recently that the number of milk producers had decreased, and please correct if I am mistaken, but I think that the number has been cut in half during the past five years. It will be stated that the producers involved are older people who have decided to give up dairy farming. This is not true, Mr. Speaker.
For instance, some forty milk producers have decided to auction their stock this year, and we are already expecting still a further spectacular and extraordinary number of auctions later on. These people know their arithmetic and they realize that they cannot at the present time support their families with what they get from their dairy operations. They have therefore decided to sell their farms.
And do not dare tell me that it is because these people are getting tired and have reached a ripe old age, that they have decided to live off the Old Age Security Pension, for it is simply no.t true! Obviously then, milk producers need normal and adequate incomes to cope with the needs of their families. I do not think Canadians will be against that. No hon. member will be against this principle either. Just how far can we go with words to try and solve these problems. I therefore urge hon. members to try and understand how important it is to solve this persistent and dangerous problem which might jeopardize the future of the milk industry in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, they also ask for one quota system for industrial milk and cream, instead of the present double system of marketing quotas and subsidy quotas. It is quite normal, logical and legitimate to give a favourable answer to such a request.
We know perfectly well that in view of the fact that the production quota is not subsidized, this results in a price that is below the cost of production. There again, those who followed the problem of our dairy industry are perfectly aware of this fact and cannot deny it. They will recognize that this is fair and true, but nothing has been done for two years in this regard. And yet, we knew long before today that dairy farmers were obliged to produce milk at a loss. Therefore, I suggest that the consumer himself will understand and will not demand that dairy farmers produce at a loss. Nobody wants to work without getting a minimum return, an adequate return. As regards those three priorities of our party relating to milk producers' requests, I hope that all hon. members will give a favourable answer and will oblige the minister to make a policy statement now rather than to wait ten more days. But if we must wait for ten days, if this is what the Canadian Milk Commission wants, then we agree to wait ten more days.
But when the Canadian Milk Commission makes its announcement, I hope that the minister who, I am sure, is aware of the situation, will respond as hon. members so kindly did. The Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellett) took part in discussions and met dairy farmers; by the way, I

read his statement which was encouraging. But there again, following their recent meeting with government members as well as Social Credit Party, NDP and Progressive Conservative members dairy farmers hope to get satisfaction because their claims are justified.
So I do hope that this debate and this chance that we have today to reply favourably to their requests will also be followed by positive action on the government's part.
Mr. Speaker, I continue reading the brief from which I select very interesting abstracts:
These things must be achieved for the 1974-75 dairy year beginning April 1st.
The major shortfalls in the present position and policies of the Canadian dairy industry are as follows:
Returns to producers of industrial milk and farm-separated cream are sharply below necessary and equitable levels: necessary to provide Canadian consumers with their requirements for industrial milk products; equitable in relation to the income milk producers must receive for their labour, their investment and their management skills.
The fluid milk consumer subsidy policy, by which the federal government has involved itself in the negotiation of fluid milk price levels to producers, has marked its entry into a field of policy from which it should immediately withdraw, ending the setting of any restraints upon the level of producer returns as a condition of payment of the subsidy.
Present policies of the federal government limit to a fixed amount the quantity of milk upon which direct assistance payments are made with the result that production of milk over this amount (which is below national requirements) is unprofitable.
Present policies of the federal government on maximum limits for entitlement to direct assistance payments for dairy enterprises are discouraging progressive producers and hindering efficiency improvement.
Present policies of the federal government are resulting in serious discrimination against producers of farm-separated cream in the returns they receive.
Federal and provincial policies for encouragement and assistance to the dairy industry in education, extension, credit and finance, and farm labour are inadequate and too often ineffective, with far too little planning and co-operation jointly with producers themselves. The industry is being severely damaged by the lack of concrete commitment by government to stability and adequacy of returns to producers in the years ahead, and a systematic basic of forward planning for the industry. Fears and uncertainty created by references to the "temporary" nature of the dairy subsidy program must be brought to an end.
There must be a sharp upward revision in present thinking by government, on the level of returns that is required in the dairy industry today compared with other occupations, farm and non-farm. Increasingly, the producers of milk for fluid consumption must be recognized as having a legitimate, vital and probably growing place in the production of milk for industrial use, and policies must be designed to take this into account.
In relation to all these matters, and in spite of representations by Dairy Farmers of Canada over recent months and indeed years in some cases, corrective action and policy has been too long delayed. The result is that the need now is for extensive decision-making and action on all of these fronts immediately. There is a critical need for early announcement of policy this year, for late-winter decision-making on production plans by producers.
Dairy Farmers of Canada is however encouraged by evidence that there is increasing appreciation by Canadian consumers of the value and attractiveness of milk and milk products in the Canadian diet. New and important confirmation of the nutritional value of milk has come forward from the Nutrition Canada Survey, and consumption of a wide range of products is rising. Canada's dairy farmers take great pride in their products and express the hope and belief that the place of milk and milk products in the Canadian diet will continue to expand.
March 22, 1974

So, Mr. Speaker, I believe that this part of the brief which has been sent to every member highlights the necessity of doing something for that industry if we intend to give sincere and serious consideration to everyday problems.
I find it is important to be responsible enough and tell the truth. We are asked to approve a cost increase and the government can reply immediately: You are asking for grants, for additional rates on account of added costs, but who is going to foot the bill?
I am right, I think, in saying that the risk involved in letting this industry go bankrupt could cost Canadians much more if the matter is not attended to immediately. I think it is important to remind consumers of the necessity to keep this industry alive for their own sake even if they had to bear part of the additional costs. If we think that this is an essential industry, we should have the courage to publicize it, to claim for a publicity that would make the consumer understand that it would be much more economical for him to pay for this increase, even if he had to pay part of it, than to let this industry die and rely on imported products that will be more expensive and which he will have to pay for, anyway.
Even if the government recognizes that such a measure would be a bad political move or a non profitable one, it has the responsibility to apply it if it is convinced that it is essential for the future of the Canadian people.
I do hope that the government will react that way and once again, I will not hide it and I do not want the consumer to believe that he will have to pay part of it, but it is up to the government, up to us as members of parliament, to make the consumer understand that it is more important to save our dairy industry and to guarantee a sufficient income to our milk producers than to let it go down, as is the case today.
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned earlier that there was a decrease in the number of milk producers and I recently learned that there will be even more auctions this spring, and this is unfortunate. It has been said that young people no longer want to get into farming in general and dairy production in particular.
What concrete steps has the government taken to encourage these young people to replace the head of the family? Of course, there have been openings for loans, but at interest rates that are way out of reach of the young farmer.
The minister recently said in committee that the young people are not interested in agriculture and wish to have a better quality of life or the opportunity to live like the young people in the cities.
I do not agree with such a statement, Mr. Speaker. For instance, it is obvious that the youth, who has seen his father face current problems and who has grown up in a family that has had great difficulty in making ends meet because the farming policies were not sufficient to give the farmers the necessary income, is worried and is reluctant to get into the business.
Dairy Policy
In my opinion, the young people could have this assurance, this security that no farmer could get compared with other labour sectors.
If a young Canadian were assured of surviving, of making a decent living, he would not hesitate to take over the family farm, but to the extent that we will offer him incentives. As regards loans, I think we should consider the possibility of granting a minimum interest rate, perhaps a respite on payment of interests for the first years and tax deductions. The role, the responsibility, the future of our agricultural industry are at stake.
In that regard, farmers and dairy producers complain about labour shortage in the summer. I invite the government to establish a youth labour bank, ensuring fair and attractive wages, thus allowing farmers to reduce their production costs so they can get the absolute minimum return they need.
Mr. Speaker, barely a day or two ago we received from the Food Prices Review Board a very interesting document prepared by Professors Fischer and MacFarlane. In its conclusion they recognize that the requests of the Dairy Farmers of Canada are justified. May I quote you an excerpt from this document:
The Board considers that the urgency of the situation requires that the conclusions of the report be brought to the attention of governments without delay. It calls on government and industry to give these proposals immediate and serious consideration as practical suggestions for the resolution of significant problems facing the dairy industry and the consumer.
Through reporting to the public in this way, the Board wishes to draw the attention of the federal and provincial governments to the strong sense of concern with which it views circumstances affecting the dairy industry which threaten the future availability of milk supplies at reasonable cost.
In this brief, Mr. Speaker, the problems of the dairy industry are mentioned, and I quote:
(1)	low financial returns to dairy producers and declining production despite substantial public support in the form of subsidies;
(2)	a lack of available skilled dairy farm labour, and the inability of dairy producers to compete with off-farm employment opportunities;
(3)	excessive seasonal fluctuations in production of milk for manufacturing which limits total annual output; and
(4)	the present high level of feed grain costs.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is important to consider all of these problems which have direct implications on the dairy industry. The government has made reference to a fair price for feed grains; nevertheless, the people responsible, that is the producers, especially in Quebec, and I think the same thing applies anywhere, are still expecting this fair price.
Last fall, we just about had standard prices and this led to a shortage in supply and the product which could be bought at competitive prices was simply not available.
All this, Mr. Speaker, is discouraging for the producer. He finds himself in a very difficult situation; he sees practically no way out. Then, we are wondering why young people are not interested in carrying on with farming. I think it is important that every hon. member should ponder over these documents, which are now available and give a favourable answer to the basic requests and to the very particular points made by the Dairy Farmers of Canada. The future of the industry throughout the country depends on it and it also assures the consumer that a

March 22, 1974
Dairy Policy
Canadian product is maintained. I think that out of pride and for the sake of a truly Canadian nationalism, we have as our duty to maintain and to preserve this Canadian resource which is the dairy industry. I do hope that all the speeches made in this House today on this matter will force the government to say yes, Mr. Speaker, I should rather say "invite the government" because they have had such invitations extended to them during the past 10 years through all sorts of briefs submitted to them. This practice of refusing to take position and introduce positive measures has caused this concern on our part and today we asked to let this House answer and speak on behalf of our milk producers. I am convinced that on both sides of the House, there are hon. members who know more on this matter than I do, and who will rise to speak to it and thus induce the Minister to give the producers a favourable answer and assure the Canadian consumers that they will be able in the future to get Canadian dairy products and will agree to pay a certain price, if necessary. There is no point in dissimulating that, but we will have preserved an industry which has left its mark and enabled many Canadians to earn their living. But since revenues are totally inadequate, we must take action as soon as possible, and not only by giving temporary grants but by adopting policies ensuring security to this industry and to the producers who have been waiting for so long.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to say a few words about the motion. Toward the end of his remarks the hon. member said there were others who would speak, perhaps on behalf of other parties who knew more about the dairy industry than he did. As to the motion itself, I am surprised it got past the office of the Official Opposition. As you will see, Mr. Speaker, the reference is only to milk. But the federal government does not have total authority in that sphere, though it does with regard to most industrial milk products. The motion refers to the "troubled dairy industry". We do not have full authority federally over the dairy industry.
I should like to comment about some of the things the hon. member said when he talked about the report of the Food Prices Review Board. There are some things about the dairy industry in that report with which I agree. He, too, seems to be in agreement with at least portions of that report. However, there is a certain amount of that famous "economists' jargon" in there with which I disagree very much. I think every dairy farmer in Canada, though, will agree with some of the things contained in that report, as well as every consumer of dairy products, too, if some study were devoted to the subject.
I hope the hon. member has the concurrence of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), and other members of his party, who think the agricultural industry can be run in a way different from any other section of society, that dairy farmers are not entitled to any increases in price and are not entitled to compensation to offset any increase in costs. He thinks farmers can inhabit a yesterworld with prices much below those prevailing in the rest of the world. I hope the hon. member has the consent of the hon. member for St. John's East to go along with our dairy policy when we do announce it.
[Mr. La Salle.)
Mr. Speaker, the dairy industry is in a bind today as I stated at the annual meeting of the Guernsey Breeders' Association here in Ottawa a couple of weeks ago. Milk production at today's prices simply doesn't pay. Let me draw the picture. Last year, milk production in Canada dropped 4.7 per cent, the sharpest decline ever recorded since Statistics Canada began gathering figures on milk production back in 1920. At the same time, consumers are demanding more milk and dairy products than ever before. Fluid milk sales increased by 3 per cent and cheese sales increased by 8 per cent.
Canada is not alone in registering a decline in milk production. The United States registered a 3 per cent decline and in New Zealand, milk production was also cut in spite of the excellent climate which that country enjoys. Production in New Zealand went down by 5 per cent. And this is where some of the experts told us, and are still telling us, we should get our dairy products-countries like New Zealand and Australia. Even in Europe, where very heavy subsidies are paid to dairy farmers, total production levelled off last October and November. In some countries it began to fall off in November and December. If the consumers of Canada think we subsidize dairy farmers, they should find out what is being done in the countries of the European community to keep up dairy production.
In spite of this situation, consumers all over the world are calling for increased milk production. The United States has met this need by lifting quota restrictions on imports. This great free trader to the south of us imposes restrictions and tariff barriers of every kind until it wants a certain product. I think a lot of people should change their minds and their ideas about these tree traders to the south. The only time that they left quota restrictions on imports, as they did for skim milk powder and cheese, is when they want a certain product. That new attitude of our neighbour to the south presents Canada with a new and growing market for our industrial milk products.
In 1973 Canada exported 27,407 purebred dairy animals, for a total value of over $20 million. Exports of dairy grade animals over 200 pounds numbered 41,268, for a value of $15.8 million. We exported 59,417 calves weighing less than 200 pounds, for a value of $7 million. I do not mind saying that I have some reservations about the exportation of so many calves. Those statistics are at once an indication that our dairy cattle are very much sought after, but it is also an indication that our producers are beginning to make more money selling the animals rather than selling dairy products.
Let me explain the reason that these animals are so valuable. Historically the price for our dairy cattle in Canada was lower than that for cattle in the United States. This trend was reversed last year and has continued this year. The 1973 values reported by breed journals on auction sales of dairy cattle going all the way from milking age females through calves with dams, bred heifers, open yearlings, heifer calves and bulls-the whole family-have increased by a full 33 per cent in 1973 over 1972. As far as I am concerned, that is a very impressive record. Those increasing values of animals are not an indicator of a failing industry, Mr. Speaker. If the House
March 22, 1974

will bear with me for a moment I will cite some more statistics to illustrate the strong position of dairying in Canada.
The values of milk production in 1972 was $773 million, but in 1973 it jumped to $900 million. The government subsidy in 1972 was $101 million and in 1973 $150 million. Dairy beef sold in 1972 was worth $300 million, and in 1973 it jumped to $350 million, In other words, farm cash receipts to dairy producers last year were up 19 per cent, from $1.1 billion to $1.4 billion.
Compared internationally, Canada ranked sixth in importance in total milk production in the world. Although production per cow in Canada in 1970 was below that of Holland and the United States, we are catching up fast. Our production per cow is way above that of New Zealand and Australia. Considering our climate and the difficulties that our dairy producers face as a result, I repeat that our milk producers are the most efficient in the world. We have the best cows, the international demand and the prices paid for the cows by other countries proves it. These other countries know the full value of milk as a food. Most of the countries buying these cattle are much poorer than Canada, such as Mexico, Cuba, many of the South American countries, Spain and Italy.
This is where the government's programs come in. Under ROP testing and breeding programs, we have bred cattle superior to those of practically any other country in the world. This has taken time, and it has also taken good programming on the part of the government and producers. They can be very proud of that. Their cattle have become so productive that this helps them to stay in business.
It was only a few weeks ago that I gave recognition to the owners of Ingholm Rag Apple President that produced a 365 day world record by giving 36,594 pounds of milk with a butterfat test of 2,098 pounds. The owners of the animal are Mr. and Mrs. Ingram from Campbellford, Ontario. These people wrote me letters and we had our government inspectors actually sleep in the barn to make sure this cow was not being fed any drugs, etc. We were very cautious in our approach because we value our ROP testing. The value we place on it is so high that we wanted to make sure that no drugs, etc., were being given to this cow.
When this cow gave this much milk, Mr. Speaker, some people said that she had just gone crazy. These people were ordinary dairy farmers, not large operators. Whenever anyone went by this cow they just gave her another shovelful of feed and she ate it. They are now trying to do the same sort of thing again. We work with these dairy farmers so that no one can doubt the records. We had seven different inspectors watching them feed and milk this cow just to make sure that the records were authentic.
These people wrote letters to me saying that they were not a bunch of thieves or crooks, that they were doing just what they should. I told them that they should protect themselves, because if this cow produced a male calf, you can imagine how valuable it would be to an artificial insemination unit. If the offspring of that calf were anything like his grandmother, then you could imagine the tremendous increase in production that could occur all over Canada. Through artificial insemination you could
Dairy Policy
increase this type of productive animal manyfold, certainly more so than was possible many years ago. It has been part of our dairy policy in Canada to do this sort of thing, and world buyers will be watching progress and bidding for the semen and the stock from the offspring of this great cow. As I say, Mr. Speaker, the owners of this animal are very proud. But this just did not happen; it needed co-operation between producers and the government in order to make sure it was done correctly. If the people concerned do not have the knowledge and the dedication that is necessary to bring this about, then an important part of the process is missing.
In this regard, many articles appear in the press about subsidies and how people are made rich. Most of them are similar to the kind of article that appeared in the Ottawa Journal last night. Although it was not about the dairy industry, we do see some written about the dairy industry from time to time. This article had this to say:
The beef subsidy should be ended. Mr. Whelan should direct his efforts to get his beef producers to be more efficient.
I do not know who wrote this baseless editorial. All I can say is, let him check the beef industry of Canada and he will find that the beef producers, the beef feedlot operators and the people in the beef industry in general are some of the most efficient operators in the world. It goes without saying that the same applies to the dairy industry. Our exotic cross-breeding programs, improvement in our feeding program and all of our research have allowed our cattlemen, not only beef but dairy, to become the most efficient in the world. I say that anyone who writes an editorial like this which tries to convey to the public of Canada the impression that beef prices are so high because we have inefficient producers should be chastised for inflaming people with inaccuracies, innuendoes and jargon. As far as I am concerned this is nothing more than a damnable lie and downgrades a paper like the Ottawa Journal, which is so worthy in many ways.
The problems faced by the dairy industry today are those of maintaining production in the face of recent large input price increases, rising returns in alternative enterprises, and a growing disinclination on the part of farmers to accept the hours of work required in dairying without sufficient compensation. I recently attended the annual meeting of a 4-H Calf Club in the hon. member's constituency of Timiskaming. It was the night for the presentation of awards. Practically every member of the audience was either a producer or the son or daughter of a beef or cattle farmer. Not one of the young people I talked to, and I did not talk to them all, had any intention of becoming a farmer. I asked one young person "Why don't you want to become a farmer like your father who has a nice farm?" He said: "I can tell you why, Mr. Whelan. I can never remember my dad taking a vacation. The vacations I have had have been with my uncle who is an electrician. The weekends when I went fishing I went with my cousin and my uncle, and he is an electrician, not with my dad because he works on Saturdays and Sundays. My uncle is away on vacation in Florida for four weeks. My dad has never gone out of the community since I have known my father and can remember. That is one of the reasons, Mr. Whelan, why I don't want to be a dairy farmer. I am not saying that my dad has not supplied a good home with

March 22, 1974
Dairy Policy
everything we needed in it, but that way of life is not for me."
There is one thing that we too often take for granted. Some people seem to think you can turn the cow off on Friday night and start it back up on Monday morning. The other day during a discussion with some officials, not from my department but from another department, one of them suggested that when you had an over-production you should cut the feed off a little bit and the cow would not produce so much milk. What a ridiculous and asinine thing to say. We know that when you cut back feed milk production does cut back, but in 99 9/10ths of the time when you increase that feed after short-circuiting it, the production does not come back. A cow is not a machine. This man thought he had a punch press or something. What he has is a machine with four spigots that depends on you taking care of it and forcing it with everything you have, including every kind of good food 24 hours a day, seven days a week. In a way, a cow is a machine but no man has invented anything that compares with a cow when it comes down to the nourishment you get from dairy products, and that is something that we in our society take so much and so often for granted.
Because of higher dairy input prices, the support levels for dairy products were raised significantly for the dairy year 1973-74. I suggest that we reacted quicker to the requests of dairy farmers than anyone else since I have been here, beginning in 1962. We reacted to their requests last year and we will do so again. In April, skim milk powder prices were increased by 21 per cent and butter prices by 4 per cent to provide an increase in the milk price of 60 cents per hundred weight, the equivalent of about 14 per cent on the average market price. In August, 1973, the dairy farmers of Canada again made representations to me for a further price increase. The return per hundred weight of milk was increased by $1 including a temporary subsidy of 56 cents per hundred weight. Dairy farmers have recently claimed that still further increases in returns are needed to offset rising input costs, and I agree that they are needed.
This government, through the establishment of the Canadian Dairy Commission and the policies handled by them, has maintained a healthy dairy industry in Canada. This government is not now about to see it go down the drain. The Canadian Dairy Commission has substantially fulfilled the objective for which it was established, namely to give efficient dairy producers an opportunity to obtain a fair and equitable return; to provide the maximum of stability for the dairy industry; to assure consumers a continuous and adequate supply of high quality dairy products, the highest in the world; to make the dairy sector more efficient by increasing the number of larger units and, most important, to secure from the market the largest possible proportion of the milk price required by dairy producers.
I want to say this about the Canadian Dairy Commission. It is a commission which was set up by this parliament, and it operates as a marketing board, no matter what anyone else wants to call it. I would challenge those people who condemn marketing boards to show that the Canadian Dairy Commission has not seen fit to make sure
(Mr. Whelan ]
that the producers get a proper return, with the result that not only has there been stabilization of the income of dairy producers, but the increase in the cost of dairy products to our consumers has been less than anywhere else.
Dairy producers have been afforded the opportunity of obtaining a fair return on their labour and investment. On production covered by direct subsidies, manufacturing milk shippers have received a return estimated to be $2 to $3 above the equivalent of world prices. In the absence of Canadian Dairy Commission programs, farmers' gross receipts from dairying would have been more than one-third lower, and the output of the manufacturing milk and cream sector alone would have been only half as large. A relatively high degree of short-term stability has been provided, both through protection from fluctuations in international dairy product markets and through compensation for the exceptional input inflation of the past two years.
Consumers have been provided with a continuous and adequate supply of dairy products of high quality. All domestic requirements of skim milk powder have been provided from Canadian milk production, and until 1972 Canada was self-sufficient in butter production. With the exception of specialty cheeses, other dairy products have been provided exclusively from domestic sources. The dairy commission has seen fit to make sure that butter supplies were adequate by foreseeing what was going to happen and importing enough butter to cover our needs.
The effort to increase the efficiency and health of the industry has resulted in a very substantial increase in the number and proportion of medium to large-size dairy operations. Between 1968 and 1973 the number of quota holders in the 3,500 pound to 17,500 pound category has increased from 32 per cent to 42 per cent of all quota holders. These people represent the backbone of Canada's dairy industry.
A few relative price comparisons between Canadian Cheddar cheese and equivalent Edam or Gouda cheese in other countries illustrates the point. In mid-January of this year a pound of cheddar cheese in Ottawa cost $1.11; the equivalent cheese in Stockholm cost $1.55; in Washington, $1.35; in Rome, $1.23, and in Australia, Canberra cost $1.24 and so on.
Let me quote some additional figures as to the retail price in December, and I use butter as an example. In 14 cities in Canada butter cost 77 cents a pound, whereas in 56 cities in the United States it cost 89 cents a pound; in Brussels, $1.24; in Copenhagen, $1.19; in lucky Ireland, 79 cents; in The Hague, $1.29; in Hamburg, Germany, $1.54; in Paris, $1.44, and in Rome, $1.60. The difference in prices is further emphasized when one compares the average earning in Italy as compared to the average in Canada. One can check the efficiency of our dairy producers by looking at the fact that with our program butter can be produced and marketed at 77 cents a pound, or it was possible to do so at that time. We cannot continue to do that, but the price will not go up to anything near $1.60 a pound.
The federal government's dairy policy for 1974-75 and beyond will be announced within the next few days. Therefore, I do not wish on this occasion to go into detail on what action the government intends to take in that

regard. I have told the farmers and have said publicly that we are working on a long-term dairy policy. Announcements will be made by April 1 according to the legislation. We are fully aware of the situation faced by our dairy farmers. I hope it is not the hon. member's intention to use the motion today for political gain, and then to say to his constituents that, when speaking in the House, he told the government what must be done for the dairy industry, and the minister is doing it. It will not do him any good no matter what he says because we have been working on it for three months as hard as we can. We have worked very closely with the dairy industry. I do not think another Minister of Agriculture has worked as closely as I have with the dairy industry. We are attempting to really find out what is needed to maintain the dairy industry.
As I said earlier it is not merely a question of economics. It is a way of life. I heard the hon. member, when speaking in support of his motion, say that he did not know much about the dairy industry. If he had to milk cows seven days a week, twice a day and before he went to school he would understand a little about the seven-day week to which I referred, which includes Sundays, holidays, Christmas, New Year's and even St. Patrick's Day. Some hon. members probably have heard about it but they would understand it much better if they actually experienced it. This is the problem in respect of some of our world programs related to agriculture.
I wonder if any hon. member has any idea how many ministers of agriculture I met who were actually farmers when I attended the FAO meetings in Rome?

That is right. I did not meet all of them because there are 132. If we say that the agricultural situation in the world is in a mess we cannot blame the farmers. We should blame the economists, lawyers and others who are trying to run the agriculture and dairy industries in the world. To say that milk is an important food is to state the obvious. It is a food that we cannot afford the luxury of expecting some foreign country to produce for us. We must forget about depending on some foreign country. We have had this experience in respect of energy when we depended on some foreign country to supply it cheaper than we could ourselves. We have had a similar situation in respect of the sugar industry.
With regard to the dairy industry, it is obvious that we must make our dairy industry capable of supplying every product we need. It is a cornerstone of our agriculture. Dairying is important for reasons other than the basic milk product. Dairy animals supply a high percentage of the beef we eat as well as all kinds of other products, everything from leather to pet food. The government is most anxious that dairy farming remain an attractive line of work for both farmers now in the business and for those young farmers whom we would like to get started in dairy farming.
Last year we doubled the amount of money spent on the dairy industry and many people in the dairy industry have confidence in what we are doing. They have confidence in this government and I am taking for granted that they
Dairy Policy
have some confidence in what this minister says. The dairy industry has its own special problems. It is a highly skilled occupation. It is not surprising then that many farmers have opted for types of farming that are a little less demanding, like beef-raising or cash-crop farming. On the way here this morning I met a man who sold his farming operation not far from Ottawa. He is 45 years of age now, and is running an elevator. He said he has a much easier life now than before and has more take-home pay. Do not forget that. One must also realize that the whole family is involved in a farming operation. What the dairy farmers need is the guarantee of a decent living over an extended period. That is why we are working on a long-term policy. This is the reason the dairy industry asked for a long-term policy to which I am committed. A long-term policy is required so that the farmers can plan ahead.
In the middle of the current dairy year, we raised the industrial milk subsidy when it became apparent that farm costs had outrun returns on the product. We did not wait until now to take action. We instituted a consumer subsidy of five cents a quart, to solve the twin problems of rising consumer food costs and diminishing net profits for the producer. The producers need long-term help as well, so that they can plan ahead and take risks in investing in buildings and in livestock with some hope that eventually it will pay off and that their industry will be what it should be and must be so far as I am concerned. I stated this in the House before. We want a dairy industry that will attract our young people and the federal government is working very hard on this right now, not only with measures already in place, but with measures to be announced soon.
The world dairy situation is changing on an almost daily basis. A few years ago, we could not give away our skim milk powder. Today, the price is about 12 cents a pound above our own support level. This is a product we use in external aid and foreign aid all over the world. That is how quickly things can change. So, while we need a long-term policy, we must remain flexible enough to react quickly to a changing situation in other areas of the world. We cannot be so fixed in respect of a plan that we cannot change. We proved last year that we would react to the needs of the producers. No matter how good our long-term policy might be, we must always be in a position to react when the producers need it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister indicated the Official Opposition, in putting forward today its motion to subsidize milk production by $2 per hundredweight, is confused because the federal government is only responsible for a section of the dairy industry, namely, industrial milk production, and the provinces have total control over the fluid milk production.
In March, the minister announced an increase of $1 per hundredweight of milk in the form of a federal support program for industrial milk production. If we added to this the $2 subsidy proposed by the Official Opposition, we would solve many problems facing the industrial milk producer. But I suggest that we should give consideration to the problem that is confronting dairy farmers, and in fact all farmers in Canada today, and ask ourselves whether or not the kind of programs we are implementing are really the programs we should be implementing.
On at least two occasions the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) rose to the emergency by putting forward ad hoc legislation which, in my opinion, has caused more difficulty than the original problem was causing, and at the same time has cost the Canadian taxpayer a great deal of money. I am uncertain whether or not it would be wise for the House to seriously consider why we are involved in subsidy programs for the dairy industry. I think it would be wise to go back several years, in fact quite a number of years, and consider the legislation that has been passed by the House. Until the last year or two the purpose of the legislation with regard to all agricultural commodities has been to provide farmers with a method of disposing of a surplus in a specific commodity. For years, Canada has been capable of overproducing practically every agricultural commodity, and nowhere has this been more evident than in the case of industrial milk production. I can remember many experiments that have been tried to dispose of our surplus products. One bright proposition which was put to parliament a number of years ago had us converting surplus butter into butter oil, but we found that there was no way of converting it back to butter nor was there any way to use it in the form of oil. That experiment proved both costly and foolish.
All of our experiments over the years have been designed to get rid of surpluses but we are no longer faced with surplus dairy products. It is true that there is an occasional surplus in powdered milk because the world is not yet willing to use powdered milk as a substitute for fluid milk, but in all other fields we find ourselves in the position of having to import many dairy commodities. This affects the consumer, and we should think what it will mean if that policy has to be followed for almost all agricultural commodities, not just to dairy products. We will shortly have to make our minds up whether we want to export water, oil, hydropower and lumber-in fact all of our raw and mostly non-renewable resources. Once we start exporting them it is difficult to regain control, so we must make the decision on whether we want the money or whether we want to maintain self-sufficiency in these commodities.
We can produce almost every agricultural commodity, from the dairy industry, from the vegetable and legume

industry as well as cereals, and under normal circumstances we can produce far in excess of our requirements. However, Mr. Speaker, we have not done that. We now find ourselves importing butter because it is cheaper to do that than to produce it. We find that it is cheaper to import almost every kind of fresh vegetable from the United States than it is to produce it here. Canadians are often shocked to see pictures in the newspapers and read accounts of apples being destroyed or not picked because it is not worthwhile to do so. We learn that tomatoes are left in the fields here because it is cheaper to import them. We have gone to great expense to develop a hot house industry in Canada, only to find that it cannot compete with Mexico or the United States when those countries dump these products here. On these occasions we have used the economic yardstick, and decided that it is cheaper to import than it is to produce.
This is particularly true of the dairy industry, and it was therefore very wise of the minister to cover the waterfront as he did. The Canadian public has not yet decided whether it is to our advantage to be self-sufficient in agricultural products or whether we should buy where the price is cheapest. At the moment, we are importing tomatoes and all kinds of fresh vegetables, whilst we are growing them and then destroying them because we do not have the ability to pick, pack, grade and distribute them.
The Conservative Party will have to consider whether it is to our advantage to pay an additional $2 to maintain the industrial milk industry. What do we do about the commodity by the time it reaches the consumer? Do we tell him he will have to pay what the supermarkets charge or do we tell him that his taxes pay the subsidy on the product or do we tell him that there is already a reasonable markup allowed in the field and there is going to be no more? This is what we have done with butter, not by design but by accident. We have done it to the extent of keeping butter in short supply. In doing so, we put many hundreds of thousands of small farmers out of business, mainly in western Canada. We got rid of the butter surplus and now we are buying butter. We will have to decide whether that is the way we want to operate our business.
I am of the opinion that if we are to subsidize the dairy industry to a greater extent, then we will have to nationalize Kraft. The hon. member who moved this motion is well aware that a very great percentage of the cheese consumed in Canada is produced and sold by Granby Co-op. That company sells 80 per cent to 90 per cent of all cheese manufactured in the province of Quebec and produces almost 90 per cent that is bought by Kraft.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
The hon. member says good; in my opinion he is being irrational. Kraft is rooking him, is rooking the Co-op, is rooking everybody in this country because they are usually selling it to the consumer at twice the price. Maybe the hon. member does not know that the floor price on cheese is something like 54 cents and that the consumer is paying between $1.09 and $1.29 for that product; that Kraft has cornered the market, put a label on the product and doubled the price. I know the hon. member is a farmer but he is willing to settle for less than half the proper
March 22, 1974

return for that commodity, even when it goes into the Granby Co-op, because he is allowing Granby Co-op to operate in conjunction with Kraft, a monopoly.
The minister will have to look at some of those monopolies in the food chain. He will have to look at the international control of the food chains and how the monopolies control the distribution of products which results in the consumer paying far more for them than is justified by the returns the producer receives. The hon. member opposite, who I am sure is going to reply, should keep something else in mind. If the farmers do not get enough money for the products they are selling, more and more of them will go out of business. I agree with the minister when he said that it is damned hard to get up in the morning and milk those cows, seven days a week, 365 days a year. We have not yet developed a good cow that will take Saturday and Sunday off or one that will give you a regular two week holiday. In fact, it will be a hardship for the milk industry if such a cow ever is developed!
It is all right for the people in the dairy. They can cut out all the frills. They can work a five day week. They do not have to milk the cow on the farm. But that does not mean that the farmer does not have to put the milk into the bulk tank after he has milked the cow. We must make sure that the farmer earns the kind of money which will enable him to live a totally different kind of life from the one farmers now live. The farmer of today is perhaps 65 or 70 years old. The next generation of would-be farmers has already opted out. Those young people are not going on the farm; they have already gone into the factories. We must talk about the second generation, the grandchildren of the man on the farm. We must make sure they can live a totally different kind of life and we must guarantee them a standard of living which will be high enough to convince the wife and family that they should live in the rural community and work the farm in a way which will guarantee Canadians supplies of food.
No matter at which segment of farming you look, you will find the farming population has been declining over the past few years. If, in the next few years, this trend is not reversed, we will not be able to choose whether or not we want to be self-sufficient. We will be forced to sell our capital assets, our non-renewable resources, and we shall find it difficult to get people to take up farming again or to resume production of renewable resources, because we shall not have the experts, the farm units or the other conditions in this country under which it was possible for farmers in previous generations to provide Canadians with cheap food.
I suggest to my hon. friends opposite that we must provide the farmer with the standard of living which will induce him to remain on the farm. We must guarantee it; otherwise, he will move off the farm. Furthermore, if the farmer is forced to provide, say, Granby Co-op or Kraft Industries with his product, and those firms sell this food in Canada at much higher prices than they pay the farmer it will be extremely difficult to convince the consumer that he ought to pay subsidies to keep the farmer on the farm. The farmer produces industrial milk, which he sells to the Kraft company. The company sells it at a very much greater price. That transfer from the farmer to the con-
Dairy Policy
sumer, with Kraft company acting as middle man, is made with no major expense to the company.

speechtext: Does the hon. member know what he is talking about?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
Well now, my hon. friend sitting in the back row is making noises, yet I assume he knows absolutely nothing about the cheese industry. If he did, he would realize that the making of cheese and butter involves a very simple process. Actually, those foods are about the simplest to transfer from the farm into the showcase. So simple are they to handle that for many years farmers used to put those products into the store and look after the counter. The mark-up in the grocery store normally was about 2 per cent or 3 per cent, considerably lower than that on other items handled by the retail grocery trade. I suggest that I have raised an important question. The problem cannot be met merely with the continuation of subsidies.
The minister, in my opinion, faces terrible trouble in the beef industry. We must make sure that the beef producer is kept in business because, once he goes out of business, it will take many years before beef production is in full swing in this country again. With producers out of business the price of beef will go sky-high because there will be a shortage. On the other hand, if we ask the taxpayer to subsidize the beef producer but do nothing to bring down the price in the store, the consumer will decide pretty soon that he is no longer willing to pay the subsidy for that commodity and will demand a totally different system for the handling of such commodities.
As I said previously, for 20 years, long before I came to this House, we faced agricultural surpluses. We designed many programs to dispose of agricultural surpluses, whether they were in wheat, butter, skim milk powder or casein. All such products, with the exception of fluid milk, have been handled on an emergency basis, because we had accumulated surpluses we could not handle. It cost too much to keep them. That situation no longer holds true. In many fields we have reached the limits on production. We have, under the present system, reached those limits in the dairy industry, as is evident if you look at the rate of production.
The minister paid a tribute to farmers for the type of cattle they are producing in this country. This has been a fabulous development of which Canada should be exceedingly proud. I can remember when I milked cows as a young lad. We had a large farm and we milked lots of cows. I can remember when we were producing a large volume of milk, but the butter fat content was less than 2.8 per cent. At that time the regulations provided for a minimum of 3.2 per cent, or you would be eliminated as a supplier. My father had to go to southern Ontario and buy two Jersey cows so that we could stay in the fluid milk business. We could not get our Holstein cows to produce milk with the required butter fat level. Today, Holstein cattle are producing milk with as much as 5 per cent butter fat. This is a great tribute to the farming community, to agricultural schools and colleges, and to farmers who have been willing to take advice with regard to ROP. They have listened, and the result has been a long period of technical development.

March 22, 1974
Dairy Policy
The farmer has done his share and often the government has been helpful. We are under an obligation to tackle monopoly concerns such as Kraft, which put little or nothing into the system, but sure as hell take out a whole lot more than their share. Unless we tackle this situation, we will find that levels of production will decrease and costs to the consumer will rise.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion of the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) is a timely one. It answers the desire of the Canadian dairy producers who want the Canadian parliamentarians to seriously study this grave problem which is now facing the dairy industry in order to help the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the federal cabinet to improve the lot of the farmers who work in this industry, the dairy industry, which is generally called the primary industry, especially in Quebec.
I would have liked myself to move a motion concerning agriculture during these opposition days, but it was impossible because of the way the time is allotted between the parties in this House. However, I wish to congratulate the mover of this motion. He has given an excellent description of the dairy problem and I am very happy to see that he supports the justified requests of the producers.
I should also like to say that I listened most attentively to the speech given by the hon. Minister of Agriculture, at least the major part of it. He dealt quite seriously with the problem and with great competence. I was impressed above all by the fact that he had the courage to say that dairy farmers are of those who cannot allow themselves holidays. If they do, they run the risk of seeing their production diminish, as well as their income, because their animals are very sensitive and must be disturbed as little as possible. They must always have the same master, and be taken care of by the same man everyday, because, when disturbed, they produce less milk; a herd of 50, 60 or 75 cows can soon lose 100 or 200 pounds of milk.
Without blaming anyone in particular, I feel that the minister does not have enough support in the cabinet. I am convinced he has done all he can and that today's debate will help find a more satisfactory solution to the dairy farmers' problems.
The situation is nothing new: as repeated time and time again in this House, the farming industry has always had many problems. It is the most important industry of all because it feeds the people.
This industry has always been the most neglected one by governments and produced the smallest income to those engaged in it. If a number of farmers can still be found today it is because they are convinced of their mission, confident that the future will bring improvements.
This industry's survival is due to the courage and steadfastness of those workers of the soil who wanted to carry out their task and who are still determined to do so but who become increasingly demanding, and rightly so, since they want their fair share of national income. In 1974 I

think it is quite fair that the farmers get the return they are entitled to.
Dairy producers have been facing the same problem for several years. They are constantly caught in the "cost-price" squeeze.
I remember that in 1967 the dairy producers of Quebec and Ontario organized a march on the Canadian Parliament so as to make the federal cabinet and parliament aware of their problems. Since I participated in this march, I remember it as if it had taken place yesterday. I was glad to be among them but at that time I was far from thinking that one day I would sit in the House and in a position to help those workers obtain justice. If I am sitting here today it is because certain reasons led me to take a more active part in the political life of my country and to accomplish as far as possible what can be expected from a dedicated member of the House who wants to improve the lot of his constituents.
Government intervention came at a certain time and mainly from 1967 but quite slowly. Progress has been slow. In 1967, the support price of butter was then amounting to 63 cents a pound. There was a slight increase in 1969 to 65 cents a pound. There was no progress in 1970. In 1971, the support price was 65 cents a pound and 68 cents in 1972. In 1973, it skyrocketted to 71 cents. It has gone up very slowly which means that dairy farmers are certainly not responsible for the cost of living increase.
In the light of the figures I have just quoted and because of the replies the Chairman of the Food Prices Review Board made to the Committee of Miscellaneous Estimates on March 14, 1974 when I asked her this: Madam, concerning the prices of dairy products, for instance, have you received any communication from consumers complaining about the excessively high prices for Canadian manufactured goods? Have you examined the situation to find out whether dairy farmers get a reasonable return, or do they in turn abuse consumers? Have you had the opportunity to go to the root of the problem?
The Chairman answered as follows, and I quote:
Yes. We expect to publish soon a very interesting brief on this industry that was presented to us. We expect to publish it as soon as the council has considered it. It is now being translated; we have already reached this stage. We keep a close look on dairy products and we have had very few complaints. I will just quote the figures: three, very few complaints; nine about all dairy products.
This means that consumers do realize that dairy farmers are not responsible for the increase in the cost of living and that they are not the ones by whom they are being gouged.
Therefore, I hope that consumers will be reassured at least in this regard, because I wanted to know whether gouging was actually exercised by producers. If consumers are being gouged, it has nothing to do with producers. Therefore, we will have to investigate that matter in order to determine whether it might be possible to improve the producers' situation without harming too much the consumer.
As I said earlier, the producer always finds himself in a bind which is called a cost, production and cost price squeeze. Over the last three years, there has been a tremendous increase in the price of machinery and spare parts. This is nonsense because users, those who must
March 22, 1974

get these spare parts, have to pay prohibitive prices, and the year 1974 is expected to be even more difficult for them.
The same applies to dairy farmers who are affected as well when they must make new construction works or repair existing buildings. For them as well as for others, the cost of materials has substantially increased.
What about labour! We have had, in February, a two day conference in Ottawa with officials of all farming organizations of this country and officials of the Department of Agriculture, and we came to realize that qualified farm labour has become scarce. It is difficult to obtain the services of skilled farm labour because young people are quite wise and are not interested in working in a sector of the economy which does not yield at least the same return as the industrial sector for instance. They are turning away from farming and this has resulted in a gradual decrease in the number of operators which in turn will very soon cause very serious food problems.
We have lived through a phoney oil shortage, but that will be nothing compared to the problems that a shortage of food products will create, if we are not determined to act now.
With regard to feed grains, it is one of the reasons for the rise in production costs. I had set nonetheless high hopes on the measures announced by the Minister of Justice on September 14, 1973, but the results have yet to come. We still experience difficulties in that respect in the province of Quebec and in the eastern provinces. Therefore I invite once more the government to study very seriously the problem, or rather to put an end to the studies and act without delay, so that the Canadian Wheat Board and the Livestock Feed Board come under the jurisdiction of the same government department, so that decisions taken in one department are not overruled by the other.
And I am convinced that our suggestion, which I am repeating again today, is worthwhile because this same minister would thus have authority to make decisions and this would settle the transportation problems.
I would also like to talk about fertilizer prices. It is a colossal disgrace. While they were set last year at $80.00 a ton, now they have reached $156, almost twice the amount.
How can farmers look to the year 1974 with optimism? And here again we wonder whether supplies will be adequate. Concerning seeds, we have the same phenomenon. I notice that even the price of every day commodities- electrical power, insurance, union fees, transportation rates-is zooming up. And accordingly dairy producers must now pay $10.15 per hundredweight to produce their milk. And at the present time producers are lucky if they can can get $7.70 per hundredweight for their industrial milk. Their deficit is therefore considerable. The farmers are asking a $2 increase. But at the time they filed their request, production costs had not reached today's level. By asking a $2 increase per cwt., they are trying to avoid what happened in the past. When the government authorized increases, the producers pocketed only part of them because, instead of getting all of the increases, a mere 25 to 30 per cent of them managed to reach them.
Dairy Policy
If possible, I should like to make a few suggestions to the minister. If the Constitution does not allow it-silly Constitution that is blocking us at everytime-why can we not amend it? It is made by people. We are no more stupid than those who drafted it in 1867. They made it in 1867 to suit them, their weight, their height. The country has grown, its population as well, and new problems have come up. And so, the Constitution should be revised so that it might not paralyze us constantly, that our administrations might become more efficient and that, in short, we might, as intelligent citizens, solve our problems.
Mr. Speaker, given the difficulties encountered by the dairy producers, the Minister of Agriculture, the federal cabinet and hon. members cannot say they were not made aware of the problem. Mr. Speaker, I will dispense from reading those briefs but I have one here dated November 20, 1973, which was submitted at an extraordinary meeting of Dairy Farmers of Canada. The attention of the authorities was drawn to the serious problem faced by milk producers. They are quite tenacious, and I congratulate them for it because they are fulfilling their mission. They look after their business and if we looked after ours in the same way they look after theirs, we would be performing very well together.
A brief submitted again to the authorities in December 1973 reads in part, and I quote:
The announcement of assistance levels well ahead of decisions regarding production is undoubtedly necessary but it must be pointed out that the further ahead the announcement is made, the more risk there is that the level of assistance itself will prove inadequate when the crop reaches the market. This makes it necessary to include in assistance levels announced ahead of time a provision allowing for a further adjustment to offset changing cost conditions. In the cattle industry, developments over the past year have made producers quite aware of the need for such a requirement.
I think that was a practical piece of advice, a quite valid suggestion so that during the year the Minister of Agriculture might say to his colleagues in the cabinet that, as regards such or such a decision, the situation has changed during the year. That is why I am respectfully submitting the necessary change so producers will not be forced to wait month after month and run into heavy debts.
In January 1974, one month later, as they do month after month, Dairy Farmers of Canada came back charging with another brief containing valid suggestions. They asked what policy should be followed and said once again, hurry up, this is an urgent matter. People are quitting production. That area is on the downgrade. On March 7, 1973, the Dairy Council of Canada submitted a paper on the problems of the dairy industry. In March 1974, another paper was submitted to the federal ministers and the Liberal members of Quebec, drawing the attention of the authorities. The farmers were told: "Hurry up." They were asked something which is never asked to large corporations which increase their prices rightly or wrongly, but according to their whims. The milk producers were asked: "Prove that you are right, show us your production costs." I am pleased to see that the dairy farmers of Canada acceded to that request and gave specific figures-
