speakeroldname: Mr. Leopold Corriveau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in today's debate which concerns a very current issue, that of the Canadian dairy industry.
Mr. Speaker, in 1973-74, the dairy industry is going through a regression period which is due to several factors of which I shall try to enumerate a few.
As concerns a first valuable solution, we know that the dairy producer needed a substantial increase, Mr. Speaker, because dairy policies are traditionally announced on March 31 of each year; as there are only a few days left to learn about these policies, I repeat that I place all my confidence in those who are in charge of making decisions in this respect and I can assure the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) that the Canadian farmers will once more be satisfied with these new policies.
The hon. member for Joliette is worried about the threatened dairy industry. I shall leave it up to my colleagues to compare today's dairy industry with the one that existed when the Conservative party was in power. I should like to ask the hon. member for Joliette if he consulted his leader before moving this motion in the House today-the hon. member for Joliette indicates that he did consult his leader-to ask that the hundredweight of milk be increased by $2 immediately, since we know that his leader may right now be telling at a press conference or on television that if he was in power, he would freeze prices for maybe 90 days.
I therefore wonder if he did consult his colleagues.
How does the federal government support the farmers in their efforts to produce at full capacity? Last year, several basic changes were made to the income tax legislation and regulations. All were designed to leave the farmer more money so that he may invest it to increase his production. Someone made a special study of those changes and made his findings known at a meeting I attended. He figured that the taxes on farm income had been reduced by almost half through those government measures. Moreover, the Farm Credit Corporation has more than doubled the amounts of loans granted last year to farmers and the government maintained a 7 per cent interest rate although the loans cost more. In addition, the federal government has increased the subsidies on certain products, has more than doubled its subsidies to the dairy industry, has increased its spendings in support of crop insurance, and has increased by more than 70 per cent its support to wheat for domestic consumption.
Finally, and what is most important, the government did not apply any price controls which would have restricted the farmers' income. In spite of this increased support, additional price increases will, of course, be necessary if dairy farmers are to meet increased production cost. I understand why the producers are considering other possibilities and are wondering whether they should sell their herds and turn to commercial farming or other farming ventures with higher incomes and less work, and yet demand for dairy products is increasing and the long-term outlook for dairy farmers has never been so good in years.
The United States have increased their imports of butter, cheese and skimmed milk powder as their produc-
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Boulanger).]
tion was decreasing. It keeps on decreasing in the United States and the demand for our milk powder and cheese is increasing there. Total American imports amount to the equivalent of 6.5 billion pounds of milk, or 60 per cent of the milk processed in Canada. No doubt that a market does exist in Canada and elsewhere and that it is expanding. It is also obvious that Canada will not be able to rely on low-price imports to meet its domestic needs, surely not in any case while demand is rising so fast south of the border. In a few years the United States will be prepared to buy all the dairy products available on international markets.
Our milk producers will require higher prices to maintain their operations and increase production. Although prices are of basic importance, there are other factors which affect dairy production, notably manpower shortages and quotas. The federal government is acting to solve these two problems. This year we intend to create farm manpower centres throughout Canada. In the beginning, we will set up 30 on a trial basis. These centres will be run by retired farmers or by people who know and understand agriculture. There will be three persons in charge of those centres: a farmer as manager, an accountant, a secretary and an assistant manager, if necessary.
The farmers who will need assistance will obtain it from those centres and the workers looking for a job can register there. The farmer hiring a worker will no longer have to bother about administrative problems such as unemployment insurance deductions, Canada Pension Plan, income tax and other paperwork since the accountant and the secretary of the centre willl handle these problems. The only thing the farmer will be required to do is send a cheque every week or every two weeks to the Manpower Centre which will take care of the rest.
If the manpower centres for farmers work as we hope they do, they will enable us to establish the number and the kind of workers we need in a specific area. If there is no manpower available in the area, we can then import workers from elsewhere, or train local people for the kind of work to be done.
The Canadian Dairy Commission will amend its regulations so that dairy producers may incorporate, which will enable them to go away for a week end, to have a holiday from time to time or to look after the herd of one of the partners who is ill or injured. The quota portion which can be subsidized has been restricted up to now to 700,000 pounds of milk. That limit was entirely sufficient for a family farm; it is not, however, for two or three families willing to pool their resources in a joint venture. The Commission will amend that regulation in order to increase this maximum for joint ventures and corporations. In order to avoid that some cunning person use an old aunt, a cat or a dog as a pretense to increase his quota, thus contravening the purpose of the regulation, the Commission will require each of the partners to be a full time producer and to have a fair amount of the capital of the joint venture. Each partner will also have to do some part of the work. We do not want this amendment to be profitable to some rich lawyers or doctors who try to evade income tax through false corporations or cooperatives. We want it to be beneficial to the real milk producers of Canada.

For too long now, the farmer has been at the bottom of the economic pyramid. The Canadian consumer has always had the cheapest food in the world. This bargain can go on under the sole condition that farmers be enabled to improve their chances of a fair and reasonable return.
It is a fact that very few people are aware of the primary role played by agriculture in the Canadian economy. Canadian dairy cattle producers now have a large export market. The exports of pure breed cattle have reached a record figure, to which a large number of non registered dairy cattle are added each year. Canadian dairy cattle are in great demand abroad.
The federal government has established a certain number of programs aiming at subsidizing our agriculture and our farmers, and these programs are largely responsible for the very low prices of food products in Canada at the present time. I do not intend to examine all of them, but I should like to give a few examples, if I may.
Through our Health of Animals Branch, we have kept our cattle free from a number of foreign diseases. The federal government has led the way by ridding Canadian cattle of tuberculosis and keeping them relatively free from brucellosis. Our cattle are among the healthiest in the world, which has contributed in reducing to the minimum the production cost and administration problems.
Our government intends to continue helping farmers meet in an objective and competent way the competition on international markets.
That is why we have insisted so much on marketing. Results are beginning to show. Farmers naturally want to take the best advantage from their relatively good position in the production of many farm commodities.
I would like to add that the Canadian Dairy Commission is constantly looking for export markets. When the United States asked for 25 million pounds of powdered skim milk, the commission was first in taking action and calling for tenders. We did all we could to obtain this market and as a result half the American demand has been supplied with the stocks of the Canadian Dairy Commission and those earmarked for trade, at competitive prices on w^rld markets. On January 25, 1974, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) announced in Ottawa the sale to Mexico of over 35,000 metric tons of Canadian powdered skim milk worth $4 million.
Here is a minister who wants to help agriculture, who does not intend to slow down his efforts to help farmers get an adequate standard of living.
That is the most important sale of skim milk powder ever achieved between Canada and Mexico. The deal was signed by the representatives of the Canadian Dairy Commission and Conasupo, the Mexican government agency in charge of purchases. That is the type of quick action that can be expected from a national marketing agency and it should give those who oppose such boards another good reason to dispute those boards' ability to co-ordinate export development efforts.
Our aim is to make the Canadian Dairy Commission the best agency in the world. It is a great challenge, but we surely intend to meet it.
Dairy Policy
The Department of Agriculture of Canada co-operates with provincial representatives in setting a better and more complete program of establishment inspection.
The federal government worked very hard behind the scenes to open the new markets we have today. Those valuable achievements have contributed to improve the status of farmers. And it is only a beginning. But now, we should certainly not rest on our laurels.
On the contrary, we are decided to continue our work even harder because we think there are even greater opportunities. Yet, I am convinced that Canadian farmers deserve at least 100 per cent of our efforts. I know that we shall have to be tenacious in order to get new and expanded markets for the benefit of Canadian farmers at home and in other countries.
Mr. Speaker, we did not dare interfere with the farm products business. We have merely passed legislation allowing provinces to co-operate in marketing in order to prevent confusion in the sale of farm commodities at the national level.
Our farmers know how to increase their output and improve the efficiency of their farm but they need sufficient incomes to invest in equipment, buildings, fertilizers and the management systems required for optimum efficiency.
For at least ten years now the dairy industry has been asking the federal government to pass measures to ensure the future of producers and stabilize their production.
In his very famous book entitled: Future Shock Alvin Toffler foretells that the pace of change will steadily increase. According to him, people, institutions, businesses and even nations that will be able to adapt themselves to change and orient it towards their own interests will be the ones that will succeed.
In the last months, we had cause to lose all our illusions about the possibilities of creating a stable dairy industry, economically independent, protected as it were against the disruption affecting other farm sectors as well as the economy as a whole. The changes that took place with regard to feed grain and protein additives were a blow to the very heart of our industry. Beef production now seems more attractive to some dairy farmers. The increasingly obvious shortage of skilled labour has checked expansion and has caused some farmers to go out of business altogether. Finally, the energy crisis affects all farmers.
The dairy industry cannot, must not be and is not immunized against change, whether it likes it or not. As a matter of fact, it even showed in the past that what mattered above all was to accept change and profit by it.
More than 40 per cent of the dairy farmers have actually gone out of business during the last five years. Still more important changes took place in the consolidation of factories and creameries. Within 20 years, the yield of a cow increased by 57 per cent in Ontario. Five years ago, only 32 per cent of the cream and milk suppliers had at least 18 producing cows. That percentage has gone up to 44 now. The rate of change increases steadily. It can still be increased. For instance, the yield per cow, which amounts to 8,000 lbs. per year in Ontario at the present time, has still not reached West Germany's figure of 8,600 lbs., that of Denmark, of 8,800 lbs., nor that of the Netherlands, of

March 22, 1974

9,400 lbs., and I must add that our own average is still far from the 20,000 lbs. registered by some Canadian producers.
The farmers' lot has also improved compared to other sectors of the economy. In ten years, the farm cost index has surely increased by 49 per cent, but during the same period, incomes have increased by 168 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that in 1962-63-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not at all sure where my hon. friend lives, but I know that what he has been saying does not reflect the problems of the dairy farmers in eastern Ontario; that is for very sure. As has happened a number of times in the past, once again the Conservative Party is acting as the conscience of the Canadian people. If the present government were carrying out its duly constituted responsibilities, there would be no need for the motion introduced by my colleague the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle).
The motion is couched in the very proper terms normally used in this august assembly, asking that the House consider reform of the dairy industry, requesting that it immediately introduce its policy and also requesting that it announce an increase of $2 in the price per hundred weight of industrial milk. That language is very fine for the heady atmosphere of the House of Commons, but in fact the farmers in my riding are the more earthy type and they want no part of that highfalutin' language. They are demanding, and rightly so, a dairy policy and saying with the conviction of years of hard labour that if it is not damn soon coming, there will be no dairy industry to worry about.
It is not very long ago that the big majority of the members of this House, and in fact the majority of the members in every provincial legislature in Canada, were either farmers or farm-oriented. This is no longer the case, and more's the pity. In those days the problems that exist now were unheard of. Simple policies made sense then. A farmer had to be allowed to earn a decent living and, as a result of his hard work, a reasonable profit-not a big profit, by a long shot. Food reached the tables of all Canadians at a price they could afford.
A product of the urban environment myself, I have made a point of becoming aware of the problems of the farmers in Hastings county. It is interesting to note that from a purely statistical point of view, the number of people on farms is down to a mere 5,000 out of a total of
65,000	in the federal riding of Hastings. This is a riding where milk and milk products form a major part of the farming area. Cheddar cheese from Hastings county, whether it is from Mapledale, Foxboro, Buelah, Eldorado Cheese factories, or as marketed by the world famous Black Diamond Cheese Company in Belleville, is without question known to be the finest Cheddar cheese in the world. Yet politically speaking, the clout of the dairy farmer has dwindled to very little, and so it is that a city

boy like myself joins with all my colleagues to demand action on behalf of the dairy farmers.
Members of the government ridicule a policy of controls and sometimes it is hard for a rightwing, free enterprise conservative like myself to accept a principle of greater government intervention. Let me show you some of the costs that the farmers in my riding are encountering now, unreasonable costs and even more unreasonable increases. If these were not in fact actually foisted upon them by an uncaring federal government, at least there is no evidence of any sympathy or assistance from that same government.
I dislike the reading of bare-bone statistics, but the numbers which I intend to quote now are more than just bare-bones; they could be the death-rattle of the entire industry. During the recent recess I made it a point, with some of my colleagues, to get even more deeply involved in the problems of the dairy industry, and the prices that I intend to quote now for 1974 are current as of four weeks ago. I have a long list of figures here and I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if I might have permission to table the list and then merely comment on it. This is a full page of statistics.

speechtext: We want to verify them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
I will give them so that you may verify them. Let us look at some of the figures. The price of cob corn increased from $61 per ton between 1973 and 1974 to $112, an increase of 84 per cent; 16 per cent dairy ration increased from $73 per ton in 1972 to $138 a ton in 1974, an increase of 90 per cent; soybeans have increased in price 100 per cent from 1972 to 1974; corn gluten, which sold at $54 per ton in 1972, now sells for $106 a ton, an increase of 96 per cent; binder twine increased from $7.50 per bale in 1973 to $23.25 in 1974, an increase of 210 per cent.
Then in respect of seed-and farmers need to seed their pasture land-vernal alfalfa increased from $42.50 per 50 pounds in 1973 to 92.50 in 1974, an increase of 118 per cent. Other types increased in this period from $46.50 to $100, an increase of 115 per cent. Hay pasture mixtures increased from 77 cents per pound to $1.45 in the period between 1973 and 1974, an increase to 88 per cent. The Canadian dairy farm type of pasture mixture increased from 72 cents in 1973 to $1.35 in 1974, an increase of 87.5 per cent. Spring grains increased from $2.75 to $4.95 per bushel in this period, an increase of 80 per cent. That is for certified No. 1 Rodney oats. Certified Herta barley, which sold for $2.85 per bushel, now sells for $5.75 per bushel, an increase of 102 per cent.
Considering the impact of those price increases, is there any wonder that the farmers are demanding an increase in the price of industrial milk? The price increase that was requested a few months ago was in consideration of the prices in effect at that time. What will be necessary to even meet costs, never mind show a small profit, is hard to estimate from day to day.
Is it any wonder that dairy farmers are going out of business? The production of milk is nothing like building widgits in a factory. If the government were to suddenly say that they would be prepared to pay a price, any price, fantastically high, for all the milk that every farmer could produce at the present time, it would not increase milk production by a single drop. It takes time and planning

and careful management. Cows are bred, the strain is improved and they grow to maturity and begin to produce milk. Barn facilities have to be prepared or reactivated. The gleaming, stainless-steel receptacles for milk fully refrigerated-cost a small fortune to install and maintain. The milking parlour of today bears absolutely no resemblance to the stable of even 25 years ago. How can we possibly expect farmers to plan three year in advance?
Here we are, on the 22nd day of March, and the dairy year begins exactly five working days from now. If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) knows what the policy for the year 1974-75 is to be, it is a big secret and he is not telling anyone, least of all the farmers who must have some information on which to base their forecasts for the coming year. It is absolutely imperative that the federal government come up with a long-term policy, fair to the farmers, one that they can bank on and one where they will know where they will be in the years to come, instead of going from hand to mouth. I ask hon. members in this House today, if they had the information that the dairy farmers of Canada have right now with regard to their future, would they invest $100,000 to a quarter of a million dollars? Would they be prepared to put their entire future in hock based on the information that has been given to us by the Minister of Agriculture so far this year?
At one of the many meetings I attended during the recess I spoke to a young farmer. Luckier than most, he had inherited some of his father's milk quotas and had a bit of a head start on some, but at 24 years of age he was looking forward to a debt that would last him beyond the year 2000, with no real certainty that it would be paid off by then. That takes a tremendous amount of courage, a lot of guts and a lot of daring considering the flimsy promises he has from the federal Minister of Agriculture with regard to any assistance for his future.
We heard the airy promises of the throne speech some weeks ago. But farmers cannot build on promises. I have letters on file too numerous to mention, from farmers of all sorts, who point out that they are actually locked in with an investment of over $150,000 and a rate of return far less than 1 per cent. They are actually struggling to make ends meet, when some of the giant corporations who market the foodstuffs that they produce are showing increasingly larger profits. I want no one to misunderstand me. I am not taking up the "corporate-bum" cry of my left wing friends, nor have I anything against profits. As I stated earlier I am, and will continue to be, a strong free enterpriser; but there is an obvious need for controls.
I am pleased that the policy of my party with regard to agriculture is also a free enterprise policy. It is a policy that demands that this government ease restrictions on lending to farmers of all ages, that will allow part-time farmers to qualify under the Farm Credit Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act. It is not unusual in my riding to have a man who sincerely wants to become a full-time farmer get up at 4 a.m., work on the farm until seven, drive to a factory where he has to work in order to keep his family alive, and after a full day in the factory return to the farm to work until nine o'clock at night.
Dairy Policy
The ARDA program must be vigorously expanded. An area within my riding and the surrounding ridings that is of considerable concern, and has been for the past few years, is the problem of the disposal of whey, a by-product of the cheese industry. At present, it is a pollutant on the land and in the streams. We have known for a long time that this material contains tremendous quantities of protein and other valuable ingredients, but despite all efforts I have not been able to persuade the federal government to participate and assist in the extraction of these nutrients for the benefit of all Canadians.
Fortunately, the provincial government of Ontario is working toward this end. I know that at least one plant adjacent to my riding is being established which I hope, by dint of the ingenuity of private enterprise and with some government assistance, will be able to produce a worth while and needed product and remove a threat to our environment. As I have said in earlier speeches on the subject, the resource material will come to around a quarter of a billion pounds annually. Certainly it is a quantity to reckon with.
Probably the most important facet of our policy is our willingness to ensure the farmer a stable price for his product provided he is willing to produce the commodities in demand. We firmly believe that farmers will produce at the maximum if they have some assurance that they will not be forced out of production during periods of high input cost and unstable world market conditions.
A strong commitment must be made by this government to a national policy of meeting Canada's dairy product needs from Canadian production, and it must be made at once. The fact that we are having to import butter in millions of pounds, and do not have enough of our fine Cheddar cheese to meet export demands, is nothing short of scandalous. In order to get this production to where it should be, there must be a sharp upward revision in present thinking in government on the level of return that is required in the dairy industry today compared with other occupations both farm and non-farm.
One of the very real costs of production is in the labour force. Recently, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) recommended that pools be formed of high school and university-age youths to meet the seasonal demands of farming. This perhaps would be an excellent suggestion, but the dairy farmer who must milk his cows morning and night, 365 days a year if he is a fluid milk producer, and almost that long if he is an industrial milk producer, needs help to provide a stable labour force where the hours of work can be shortened and the pay improved so that wages are more in line with income available from alternative employment.
We talk about energy shortages and other international problems. These are serious problems. But does anyone have any idea what the crisis would be like if the housewife in the supermarket, no matter how much money she has in her hands, could not purchase enough food? This is a very real possibility if the farmer is not assisted to remain on the land. Frankly, I do not know how to state this dread possibility strongly enough.

March 22, 1974
Dairy Policy
At one of the many meetings I have referred to, a veterinary not too many years old, but with a wisdom well beyond his years, stated the problem in a way that no city boy representing the farmers could ever do. I shall try to quote Dr. Murray to the best of my ability. This is what he said: "All the statistics, the input costs, the marketing schemes probably completely miss the point. We are no longer dealing with an old-timer who came through the depression when milk was 50 cents a hundred weight. No matter how tough times get, he can always refer back to those days and decide that the present situation is at least better than that. Those farmers were patriotic, but they were only a couple of generations removed from the old country. During the war they produced food out of patriotism. Ceilings were removed from labour costs after the war, but not on food. The old-timer took the attitude that times were worse during the depression and he went on producing."
"In the past some organizations have tried farm strikes, but they failed because of the dedicated old-timer's patriotism. But these men are quietly fading from the scene. The educated sons are taking over, and if our educational system has done nothing else it has taught this generation that you don't do one damn thing unless you get paid for it. They'll try farming, but unless you lay some of that green stuff on the palm of their hand they quit and do something else. You and 1 have got to show these young men that they can make a living, plus interest on their investment, and if not we will have no farmers tomorrow. This is what has to be done." Those words, from one of the wisest men in the dairy industry whom I have ever encountered, sum up the situation pretty well.
We must have new and aggressive policies that will reverse the trend of Canadians leaving the farms. The aim must be to bring the terms and conditions of life in the agricultural sector up to par with the financial and other returns of urban existence. The Canadian agricultural industry and all its allies and subsidiary components basically require two ingredients for economic stability. These are: a constant market for its product and a fair margin of profit on the labour and capital invested. If today's evidence of the problem of uncertainties in rural food production and in the world economy teaches anything, it must be that we must have a regular and dependable supply of food products from Canadian production. Not to utilize the great agricultural resource base of Canada to produce our own dairy products would be a tragedy.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
I think it is a very important resolution that is the subject matter of this debate, but it has wider ramifications than just the production or the cost to the consumer of one particular product. Of course, what we are referring to chiefly in the motion is manufactured milk, and for a few moments, I wish to refer to the

problem with regard to its special application in Prince Edward Island, the area from which I come, where the agricultural industry consists mainly of mixed farming, a very important element of the success of which is the dairy industry. This is true in many of the older and more settled parts of Canada. I believe the same is true in the province of Quebec. The income from dairying is an important factor in the life of an agricultural area. I can imagine urban people who have been cut off from the countryside for a generation or two becoming a little tired of hearing farmers like myself and others in the House- we are diminishing breed both in the House and in the country-complain about what they think is our particular problem.
Madame Speaker, in my opinion this is not just a problem of dairy farmers; it is not just a problem of farmers; it is not even just a problem of rural Canada. It is a problem that has far wider ramifications and implications than that. This problem concerns all Canadians. It concerns urban people, and I hope they realize this, even more than rural people who are the producers of dairy products. Although the first impact may be felt by the producer, a worse impact will inevitably fall upon the urban dweller if we do not have national policies that make good sense.
Recently, a royal commission in Prince Edward Island known as the Adams royal commission made a report on the dairy industry in that province. I should like to quote from the introduction and observations as follows:
While there can be little need to remind dairy farmers of the fact, it is worth making the point for those who have never had the pleasure, that dairying is a particularly demanding occupation. In a society becoming increasingly leisure conscious that seven day a week nature of the business is not one that is accepted lightly. This fact has two very important implications which are frequently overlooked. Firstly, those in the business have a particularly clear right to fair and stable prices and that, secondly, if this is not forthcoming and they leave it, there is no endless queue waiting to fill the vacancies. Given this and the fact that dairying brings in about one-fifth of total agricultural income in P.E.I., and failure on political, partisan or prevaricatory ground to take the steps which are necessary to resolve the industry's problems will be especially unforgivable and extract a price which will be heavy and shared ultimately by every citizen of the province.
I believe that these remarks apply nationally as well, because many people, including the minister, have said this is not an industry that can be turned on and off at will. This is an industry in which there has to be a reasonable expectation of security before young men will enter it and produce dairy goods in the years ahead; I was going to say "for future generations" but that is looking unnecessarily far into the future. If we do not ensure this, the dairy products required for the nutrition of Canadians will not be available within the next decade. We are already importing large amounts of butter and some other dairy products.
There is another very important side effect, and this is especially true in the mixed farming areas of Canada, the backbone of rural Canada in a way; and that is not to deprecate the one-crop experts who frequently operate large areas growing specialty crops such as wheat and tobacco. I refer to the family farm, what we think of as the rural life of Canada, for whom a stable market for dairy
March 22, 1974

products is a necessity, just as the products themselves are a necessity for Canadians.
The royal commission report continues:
The dairy industry is of very considerable significance in the total agricultural picture in P.E.I. Although over the last decade there has been a steady decline in both cow numbers and total output, cash income from dairy producers has remained fairly stable at around 15 per cent of total cash income from farming. Its importance, in fact, goes much beyond the actual cash receipts which show up in statistics. This arises from the fact that the year-round income from dairy cattle is a very important stabilizing factor to both the cash flow and general economic health of many farmers and the fact that the further processing of the product takes place on P.E.I. results in the creation of many more jobs and increased economic activity.
Over the last ten years there has been a fairly steady decline in the numbers of dairy cattle on farms in P.E.I. In 1971 the number was down to approximately 28,000 cows and heifers of two years and older, which compares with a figure of 35,000 in 1967 and 39,600 in 1961. Over the same ten-year period, total production of milk declined from 227 million pounds to 198 million pounds.
The report goes on:
Thus in 1967 no less than 66 per cent of all census farmers in Prince Edward Island ... were deriving part of their income from the sale of either cream or milk.
Possibly of even greater significance is the fact that while between 1967 and 1972 the number of census farms declined by approximately one-third, over the same period the number of milk producers was halved and fell to 48 per cent of all census farmers.
The dairy aspect of farming in my province has been so unsatisfactory that those engaged in it are leaving at a greater rate than people in other types of farming. The criticism that I am about to make is not a partisan one, but for many years I have felt that the machinery of government is terribly deficient in evolving agricultural policy and rural policy in general. The reasons for this are difficult to pinpoint. I think it is because governments take most of their advice from experts in economics, in statistics, finance or some related field and they do not really understand the implications when they try to apply this advice to agriculture or to the rural philosophy of society in Canada. There is not enough input from rural Canada.
Time and time again governments, with the best intentions in the world, evolve policies which have a bias in favour of urban Canada written all over them. I think one of the greatest tragedies that history will show, and indeed it is still happening, is that Canada has become so urbanized over such a short period of time in a few large centres. This has created, and will continue to create, great problems for us as a nation in all areas, from crime to pollution, food prices to the price of land for homes, and everything else.

speechtext:
Madame Speaker, this is one small aspect of the general problem. People, especially young people, have been driven off farms and out of rural Canada and have crowded into cities. Often they have created problems with regard to employment. Those problems do not affect them, as usually those who migrate have attained an educational standard and standards of health, ability, intelligence and responsibility which enable them to find employment. Nevertheless, their migration increases competition for jobs available in urban centres. That is only one factor which must be considered if we are to maintain a healthy rural society which will be attractive, especially to young people who are growing up and being educated on farms.
Part of our mistake has been that in the past few years we have worshipped false gods, or golden calves: perhaps I had better say that since we are talking about the dairy industry. We have been sold a bill of goods. We have been told that size is equivalent to what is desirable, that progress is synonymous with growth and that a healthy economy must grow rapidly. It is elementary to observe that nothing can grow indefinitely. Things which grow too large and too long collapse under their own weight and become extinct, like the dinosaur.
It is obvious that Canadians, both urban and rural-dwelling, want a high quality of life in a suitable environment. They want to be reasonably free from pollution and from anxieties created by crime. If they can look forward to reasonably priced housing on land which can be bought for reasonable prices, instead of for prices which are so high because demand is greater than supply and they are being gouged, and if they can look forward to a reasonable diet at a reasonable cost, the prerequisites for the good life will have been met.
Yet, as someone else said, man does not live by bread alone. We must consider the sociological aspects of this rural and urban problem. One aspect, of course, has to do with the dairy industry's troubles which we are considering at present. We must look at the whole picture and make sure we act in such a way as to lessen the economic difficulties of farmers, especially dairy farmers, so that there will not be the continued migration of people from agriculture generally and from dairy farming in particular. If present trends continue much longer, the countryside will be almost totally depopulated. Cities will be overcrowded and their inhabitants will pay exorbitant prices for food much of which probably will be imported from other countries. That situation is totally unnecessary.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
I should like to take the opportunity to place on record some of the thoughts which came out of a meeting we held with members of all commodity groups in Huron county a short time ago. It was a valuable meeting. One is held every year and members of parliament are brought up to date with regard to the problems facing people engaged in agriculture, which are varied and many.
There has never been a time in recent years when there has been greater need for clearcut and decisive action by government in the field of dairy policy.
It will not be good enough in 1974 simply to carry on existing programs or to make only minor changes in them. What is needed are major policy commitments and initiatives. Figures issued by the Canadian Dairy Commission show that between September, 1972, and September, 1973, 2,179 producers left the dairy industry in Ontario alone. That represents 8 per cent of the producers in this one province. In Quebec, 3,174 left the dairy industry, representing 10 per cent of the producers in the province. These two provinces account for the majority of the production of dairy products in Canada.

Dairy farmers all over Canada face similar problems regardless of where they live. They have to put up with long hours and a seven-day work week. The cost of all their inputs has greatly increased. They are faced with demands for higher wages, increased unemployment premiums and higher compensation premiums in an industry where it is almost impossible to find reliable help, partly because the government pays people more not to work than the dairy farmer can afford to pay them for working.
Feed costs have risen beyond the range of a dairy farmer who does not benefit by a big acreage on which to grow his own grain. Mixed grain is selling at almost $105 a ton, and corn at $3 a bushel. Soybean meal costs more than $200 a ton and can be grown only in a few parts of Canada. Prices of all the other feeds are in the same range. The ratio of industrial milk returns to 24 per cent dairy supplement in Ontario dropped from a level of 1.87 in November, 1971, to a low of .85 in July of 1973.
The lack of confidence which has contributed to this massive exodus from the industry must be dispelled by the creation of a long-range dairy policy in which producers will be reassured as to their future. We heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) suggest today that the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. LaSalle) was playing politics when he introduced his motion, because the minister had told the House in answer to a question a day or two ago that he was planning a long-term dairy policy.
Over a year ago, as reported in Hansard for March 26, 1973, I asked the Minister of Agriculture when he would be announcing his dairy policy and whether he would extend it for more than one year in order for producers to plan their production better. Further than that, I believe the records of the Standing Committee on Agriculture in past years will show that I have suggested that this be done when the Canadian Dairy Commission or former ministers have come before the committee.
My people suggest a five-year program in dairying which would be announced in advance and updated annually, coupled with a program to develop and use an economic return formula for industrial milk. This would ensure an adequate level of returns and a greater degree of confidence and stability in the industry to both producer and processor, as well as providing the consumer with an adequate supply at all times.
There is need for an immediate increase in returns to producers of industrial milk. The dairy farmers' convention in Regina voted a $2 per hundredweight increase for industrial producers, suggesting approximately $1 per hundred come from the trade and a $1 per hundred subsidy. If the consumer subsidy on fluid milk of five cents a quart is not a long-term government policy, then perhaps it should be phased out in such a way that it has a minimum market impact. We are all aware, as has been mentioned previously in this debate, that imports of milk products, particularly butter, have been increasing. In the last dairy year we imported more than 50 million pounds of butter. For a country like Canada this seems wrong and only indicates that past policies have not been adequate to encourage producers to stay in production in order to meet the demand of consumers.
March 22, 1974

Another problem that arises is that when the production of milk gets low, processing plants that process milk powder and butter are only able to operate a few days a week rather than full time. This inevitably raises the cost to consumers, while the producer receives nothing in terms of compensation.
Another matter I should like to mention is the recent seven cents subsidy provided to beef cattle producers. This is harmful to the dairy cattle producers. I say that because we all know that half of the cattle that are calved in the dairy industry do not produce any milk but inevitably are used for beef and a few are used for breeding. The seven cents subsidy announced a week ago today is of no advantage to most dairy cattle farmers because their cattle do not fall within the A-l, A-2, A-3 or A-4 category but, generally speaking, would be marketed as grade B or grade C cattle, or in other words commercial cattle.
I do not know whether the Minister of Agriculture gave any consideration to this fact, but I suggest this is discrimination. These dairy farmers feel they are beef producers just as much as anyone else. Further to that, when the seven cents subsidy was put on, the market dropped by over half of this seven cents subsidy, so one can easily see that those who could take advantage of the subsidy immediately lost half of it, about 3.5 cents a pound. This is probably one consideration that the Minister of Agriculture and the government did not take into account before the subsidy was announced.
Since the subsidy was announced we have seen great havoc in the cattle industry and in the marketplace. I am advised today that in some markets in Canada, cattle are being sold with the seven cents a pound being added after the sale; and other markets cattle are sold with the seven cents a pound included in the price. I ask, how can an industry operate in such a fashion? It seems to me some consideration should have been given to farmers with dairy cattle such as Holsteins, Guernseys and Jerseys that are sent to market and form a large part of the income of our dairy farmers.
The loss of 3V4 cents a pound to the cattle producers has generally come about as a result of the lack of thought given to the situation before the announcement was made. This has caused great difficulty but is typical of some of the actions the government takes. It would have been much better for the industry had the government provided some protection from imports, which I believe is what the industry asked for. Certainly this is where the original problem arose. The minister said the government did not want to take action against imports since it had put a tariff on imports previously and had been charged for the damage suffered by United States producers. This was damage suffered as a result of the tariff put on by the government a few months ago as a short-term measure to assist the beef producers of Canada.
I suggest that that is a very poor excuse. If the government is being billed for any damage done to U.S. producers from the surcharge the government imposed, then I hope it will refuse to pay the charge levied against it. If it does not, then it will appear to be just as uninformed and to have the lack of business knowledge that a lot of people in this country think it has.
Dairy Policy
May I also point out that many milk producers in this country also raise hogs. According to letters I have received lately, the hog producers are in a similar situation to the beef producers and are faring just as poorly in terms of returns from the marketplace. The cost of their feed is equally as high. We all know that beef and pork compete for the same market and you cannot lower the price of beef without this also having some effect on the price of pork. People are wondering what the government is going to do to assist the pork producers similar to the way the beef producers have been assisted, even though the assistance was given in a way that did not do the most good.
Let me read from a letter I received recently in regard to the cost of producing hogs. Perhaps I could put a few of these costs on the record so that our consumer friends may realize that the production of pork is not all roses. This gentleman states in his letter:
In regards to our phone conversation of this evening I am enclosing some figures on our cost of production. We have a farrow to finish operation. It takes 14 bushels of corn and 200 lb. of soyameal and mineral pre-mix to produce a pig-this includes feed for the sow, boar, and starter and finishing. With corn at $3.20 per bushel and soya at $200 per ton and pre-mix at $270 a ton, our cost for feed totals $66 for each hog we produce. The market at present in Toronto is $45 per hundred pounds of dressed weight-which is returning approximately $70 a pig. We are now faced with the position of having $4 per head for labour, interest, building, equipment, medication, insurance, profit, marketing, hydro and fuel-leaving us with a loss of approximately $12 per head. We market about 1,200 a year.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should suggest that this man is never going to become a millionaire when you consider those costs of production. He goes on to say:
As I stated on the phone, I don't mind competing with any producer, whether beef or pork, but when it comes to competing with the government and its treasury, I am afraid I just don't have that kind of money.
I suggest that the hog producer requires some kind of protection and I do not think it should be provided by lowering the price through government subsidy, and that is actually what has happened as a result of government subsidy, although many consumers are not willing to admit it. This man then says in his letter:
I have the plans for a new building, and the contractor ready to go, but I just can't justify going ahead if I have to work against these odds.
Thank you for your phone call-it was much appreciated. I have enclosed these figures so that you could see our position more clearly.
I hope the minister will consider that situation and will see what he can do in respect of hog production. I hope we will make some change in the method he adopted in his attempt to help beef producers.
There are one or two suggestions I wish to put on the record in the hope that the minister will give them further consideration before making his policy announcement in respect of the dairy industry. I listened to the words of the hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cote) and noted that he did not make many suggestions but spent most of his time condemning the hon. member for Joliette. A similar situation existed yesterday at the meeting of the miscellaneous estimates committee: members from Quebec seemed to spend much of their time ridiculing Conservative members rather than trying to obtain opinions from the wit-
798

March 22, 1974
Dairy Policy
nesses or express policies of their own. It became obvious to me that some members across the way from Quebec have been stung a little bit and do not have things the way they used to have them. They do not have their own way all the time, as they once did. I apologize for those remarks and must say that I am very seldom political, because that is not my nature; but I could not help noticing these things.
The Canadian dairy producers have stated that they require an immediate commitment from the government of Canada to a national policy in order to meet Canadian dairy production, and that three essentials are required. They require an over-all increase in returns to industrial milk and cream production equivalent to at least $2 per hundred pounds of milk. This is a figure that seems to be agreed to by everyone, but we do not know whether it has been agreed to by the government.
In addition, the dairy industry requires a commitment by the federal government, preferably by parliament in legislative form, to the future maintenance of income for milk production at fully adequate levels. I suppose that will have some reference to the ten-year program about which the minister has spoken, and I hope this is taken into account when he makes his announcement.
The industry suggests that it needs a single quota system for industrial milk and cream, in place of the present two-part market share quota and subsidy eligibility quota system.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I appreciate very much the indulgence of the House. I should like to close by suggesting that a national dairy policy for Canada should be designed so that the requirements of the Canadian consumer for milk and milk products is met, with few exceptions, by Canadian production. Such a policy must be maintained in view of today's uncertainties in world food production. If evidence of these uncertainties in world food production and in world economic conditions teaches us anything, it is that it would be the worst kind of mistake to sacrifice a policy of regular and dependable supply from Canadian production for the imagined and, to say the least, highly uncertain benefits of a policy allowing the Canadian industry to decline, with increased reliance on imports. Not to utilize the great agricultural resource base of Canada to produce our dairy product needs would be a tragedy indeed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is nice to note on a quiet day like today that hon. members of the House of Commons are finally united in one fact, namely, that farmers have to work seven days a week and cows have to be milked twice a day, including Christmas day, Easter and all the other holidays that other people normally enjoy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext: Including June 24.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
It is nice to note, also, that we are united in the fact that no one in our society works harder than those in the agricultural industry, and this means not only the man of the house but the mother and the children, in many instances. The farmers of Canada, not just those in the dairy industry, work as a family unit, with the result that in many instances the mothers work harder than many fathers in other branches of society.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis) is not present to hear what I have to say. In his enthusiasm in pointing out the fact that he places so much importance on the agricultural industry, he overdid himself by suggesting that the Conservative Party acts as the conscience of the Canadian people in respect of the dairy industry. Let me suggest that for the first time in our history we have the conscience of the people of Canada, in respect of the agricultural industry, sitting in the House of Commons. I would be the first to admit that inasmuch as the Liberals have been in government more than any other party, we have had more Liberal ministers of agriculture than any other party. But having said that, let me point out that for the first time since 1867 we have a Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who is the real conscience of the agricultural industry.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK

speechtext:
We will let that remark rest where it deserves, Mr. Speaker. Just this morning the Minister of Agriculture said, "the dairy industry in Canada is in a bind". He admits it quite frankly. There are no politics in that. He says that the dairy farmers in Canada at present are not getting a square deal. He has travelled across Canada from Vancouver to Newfoundland and told the vegetable growers, "You do not have a square deal". He told beef farmers, "You do not have a square deal, but I will get you one". He told the tobacco farmers, "You do not have a square deal". This morning in the House he told the dairy farmers, "You do not have a square deal, you are in a bind; but I will see that you get a square deal".
Granted, if you want to play politics all down the line, the minister has not been 100 per cent, successful. Granted, as my friend the hon. member for Huron (Mr. McKinley) pointed out, the seven-cent beef subsidy that was initiated one week ago today has not been 100 per cent sucessful. But one thing the farmers of Canada know is that the seven cents subsidy is a whole lot better than nothing; and it was given by the Minister of Agriculture who convinced his cabinet colleagues that this was good for the beef farming industry, and he will do exactly the same for the dairy farming industry, as will be announced in the next few days. Have no doubt about that whatsoever.
The minister does not intend to see go down the drain this great industry that is so necessary to all of us as Canadians. This morning he told us many of the problems that he has and that the dairy industry has in Canada. He pointed out, and rightly so-this has been emphasized by every hon. member who has spoken-that the number of dairy farmers in Canada is decreasing. One of the reasons for this is, not the price of dairy products even though the price should be upgraded but that all farmers have not decided that from now until they go to their natural graves they will work seven days a week. In fact, they have decided not to do it. This is not a peculiarity of Canadian farmers; it has happened all over the world. As was pointed out this morning, in New Zealand the rate of decrease in the dairy industry is more substantial than in Canada. However, we have enough problems here in Canada without thinking about our New Zealand friends, although it is always good to make comparisons.
Something must be done about the dairy industry in Canada, and much has been done in the past by the present government. But the time has come when even more must be done and will be done, I hope, within the next week or ten days or so. As has been pointed out by members of the opposition and members of my own party, it is not right that a country as huge as Canada, the second largest in the world, as sparsely populated as we are, should have to import 56 million pounds of butter as it did last year, particularly when we remember that five years ago we had so much butter that we did not know what to do with it, and we had so much powdered milk in storage that we did not know what to do with it. We were trying to give it away or to sell it at six cents a pound. But today the price has increased substantially and we can sell it at a good profit.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
But you drove the small dairy producer out of business.
Dairy Policy

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED NEED FOR DAIRY POLICY AND INCREASED SUBSIDY FOR MILK
speechtext:
It is still not right that we have to import large amounts of butter. People who are not engaged in the agricultural industry should remember that last year, if my figures are correct, we imported butter from New Zealand and Australia at 58 cents a pound f.o.b. Vancouver. It came in huge blocks. From there it was taken out to various dairies, put into one-pound packages and distributed across Canada. The significance lies, not in the fact that the butter went for 58 cents a pound but in the fact that the year before the price was substantially lower, and that next year it will probably be substantially higher.
I say to all the armchair critics, particularly to people who quoted the Minister of Agriculture this morning, such as the famous Tory paper, the Ottawa Journal which stated that so far as farming is concerned we should have greater efficiency, that if the Ottawa Journal had the efficiency of our farmers it would have a larger subscription rate than the Toronto Star and, as my friend here says, they would not be printing such silly editorials indicating that we must have greater efficiency in the agricultural field. Of course we can do better, but the fact is that we are the best in the world in so far as efficiency in agriculture is concerned. Our farmers demand that they be paid for it, and at the same time some of them go out of business because they feel it is easier to be an electrician, a politician, a preacher or a teacher. From what I can see, coming as I do from an agricultural area, any one of those professions is somewhat easier.
My friends who brought in this motion today did so possibly with good judgment, because we all admit that the dairy business is not the best in the world. However, it is the most efficient and the cheapest. The Minister of Agriculture indicated some prices. This is a fact that I wish the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) would remember. Unfortunately, he is not here this afternoon. The minister pointed out that last year butter cost, on the average, 77 cents a pound. In Copenhagen, the capital of one of the greatest dairy producing countries in the world, Denmark, it is approximately $1.50 a pound. The only nation that could approach us in the price of butter was Ireland, which was two cents higher, 79 cents. The United States was about 89 cents a pound, and in Rome, Berlin and Paris butter was almost twice the price it was in Canada. When people say that the farmer or the industry is making too much money, let me tell them that compared to the rest of the world we can hold our heads very high.
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take up much time this afternoon. Like most other members who have spoken, and the Minister of Agriculture who spoke this morning, I agree that much more must be done in order to keep our dairy farmers happy and in business so that we as consumers can enjoy Canadian dairy products in the years to come.
The hon. member for Hastings is not here, but when he spoke he was quoting the prices that dairy farmers were having to pay for the things they need, such as hay. He said hay has gone up by 87 per cent or so. Where does he think hay comes from? It comes from the farmers. So I think he picked a very poor product for an example. I know many hay farmers in the province of Ontario who

I know many farmers in Ontario and the western provinces who are pleased that the price of seed has gone up. There are many things that we can be critical of, but when farmers are feeding produce to their dairy cattle I do not think they should be too serious in their condemnation of such things as hay and seed.
I am content to leave myself in the hands of the fighting Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Speaker. Unfortunately, he could not be here this afternoon. He is away fighting for farmers and agriculture this afternoon and will make two speeches tonight. My advice to my hon. friend is, read those speeches and see what it is like to have a man who when he walks along that fence is not afraid of falling off. Every farmer in Canada knows whose side the minister is on. He is on the side of the farmer, including the dairy producer whose battle all of us are fighting this afternoon.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity that this motion presents to make some comments and suggestions to the government on the importance of the dairy industry in Canada, and more particularly as it relates to the highly productive area of southwestern Ontario. It is interesting to hear my colleague from Bruce (Mr. Whicher) relate how well the government understands the industry. I hope he stays and listens to what I have to say.
My riding can claim the second highest production of No. 1 milk in Ontario, with somewhat over 150 million pounds annually. We also have a very high dollar value of industrial milk shipments, as well as sending dairy replacement stock all over Canada and the world. I was interested in what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) had to say to the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) this afternoon. The minister severely criticized our party, trying to make us believe that it should have been unthinkable for us to even suggest devoting an opposition day to a subject that we should know his department has well in hand.
We are well aware that the minister is obligated to present his dairy policy by the first of the month, but we are also well aware of the disastrous results of the minister's current announcement respecting the beef qualify premium program. We just could not sit idly by, merely keeping our fingers crossed and hoping that when the first of the month comes we will hear a dairy policy from the minister that does not leave a lot to be desired.
The minister claims that nothing said today will change the policy which is expected to be announced next week. But remember, he had the nerve to come into this House a week ago and make a statement on a beef policy and then come back three days later with the guidelines to accompany that statement. I say, Mr. Speaker, that his department might well take into account what is said in this debate because they still have a week to go before making the dairy policy statement.
When the government recognized that the farmers of this country would listen to and accept the statements of the Minister of Agriculture he was encouraged to travel back and forth across the country, covering many thousands of miles. Being a great ambassador for the govern-(Mr. Whicher ]
ment, I am sure he enjoyed it. But I am also sure that the farmers are beginning to wonder, particularly the beef producers, just who or what went wrong in his department. There could not have been much research or forethought before the minister made his brief announcement last Friday afternoon. It immediately started the phones ringing in every rural riding. The big question is, where do we go from here? I am willing to believe that the first announcement was all the department intended to release, but when they started to get the flak, the minister then agreed on Monday that he would have a set of guidelines hopefully before the day was out.
There could be a whole debate on this one point alone, Mr. Speaker, but I do not intend to dwell on the confusion of not only the beef producers and retailers but urban consumers as well when they see the millions of dollars that are being spent on the program. My reason for mentioning this example is to emphasize to the government and to the minister that with the representation this party enjoys right across rural Canada, we could not sit idly by and keep our fingers crossed that yet another subsidy program will be announced without attempting to impress the government of its importance.
In his remarks the minister said that he hopes this motion is not just for straight political purposes. That kind of statement reminds me of one made in similar vein by the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) in committee the other day when he tried to give the impression that the official opposition was the only party that resorted to political trickery. Mr. Speaker, I hope my friend had his tongue in his cheek when he said that. All anyone has to do is read some of the records of parliament the last time the Liberals were in opposition. Any so-called political trickery that our party might be accused of would look like a Sunday school picnic compared with those days.
I should like to contain my remarks, in the time I have left, to refer to some of the problems of dairy producers in Ontario and more particularly southwestern Ontario, the area I know best. First of all, I should like to say something about the cream producers. I am given to understand that there are around 4,500 cream producers in the province. Perhaps the on-the-farm cream producer did not modernize as years went by and enlarge his production from the time when the majority of milk production was handled by separating the cream on the farm.
Statistics Canada reported that production of creamery butter fell by 2.4 per cent in February to 10.2 million pounds from 10.5 million pounds a year earlier. Mr. Speaker, the cream producers are asking for about the equivalent of $1 per hundred pounds over the $2 already asked for by the industrial shippers or, in reality 30 cents per pound of butterfat. I can see where some concentrated effort to encourage cream production can be very important in order to supplement the income of a family living in the country, with the breadwinner working in town in the daytime but coming home at night to milk a few cows. He would not have to do it by hand either, as there are all kinds of used milking machines on the market today. He would then only have to separate the milk, which would give him the most natural protein supplement which is available-skim milk. He could keep a few sows, which in
March 22, 1974

turn would produce litters that he could fatten with very little more than home grown grain plus the very valuable skim milk.
Even though the minister is, or has been, a practical farmer, as important as any increase which farmers can get for their product, be it cream, milk or any other product, is the fact that more stress should be put on more practical approaches. Let us have such approaches instead of the grandiose plans that economists have dreamed up in some departments in order to justify the huge salaries that we have seen included in the estimates in the last few days.
I listened with interest to the minister's remarks this afternoon. I agree wholeheartedly with many of his comments, particularly those in which he compared what we pay for cheese and butter in Canada with what people in other dairy producing countries pay. I also agree that many Canadians do not realize the high level of subsidies paid to producers in other dairy producing countries. What is bothering most of us in the opposition and most of our socialist friends to my left who are partners in a coalition caucus is the fact that the Minister of Agriculture is not putting his message across to the rest of the cabinet. They do not seem to recognize the importance of agriculture.
Today in his speech the minister asked how many of his international colleagues who attended the agricultural congress in Italy were farmers. The answer, of course, is that none of them were. Instead of worrying about how many of his colleagues who attended from around the world are farmers, he should be trying to convince other cabinet members of this government of the long-term importance of agriculture for Canada. In particular, he should be trying to convince the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray). Further, how the government can justify making one minister responsible for the Department of Justice and the Canadian Wheat Board is beyond me. Of course, we must not forget the congenial Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand). He, too, should be thoroughly aware of what agriculture means to this country.
As I said earlier, I want to make suggestions as to how the dairy industry can be improved in Ontario, particularly in my own area. First and foremost, of course, we must consider the price of milk. It must be sufficiently high to enable the farmer to carry on. Sometimes, the farmer's net income can be affected by factors which may be far more important than the price he receives per hundredweight of milk. He must consider the price he pays for dairy equipment and machinery necessary for feeding his cows. He must make a sizeable investment in all sorts of equipment if he is to carry on the dairy farm.
Dairy Policy
As I say, what he has to pay for equipment and for his total investment may affect his income in a direct way.
Let us consider what the average dairy farmer must invest. There has been much talk of the expertise in this country in the area of dairy farming. What do you need to operate a dairy farm? My people have operated a dairy farm for a long time. We were in the business a long time before I became involved in politics. Let us look at some of the investment necessary to enable the dairy farmer to operate a dairy farm. First, he needs between 300 and 400 acres of land. In Ontario that land will usually be near urban areas. This situation has arisen from the fact that in earlier days dairy farmers had to be close to urban centres because of difficulties of transportation. Consequently, such land today is very expensive. Being near an urban area, it could cost between $400 and $500 an acre, so his land would cost in the neighborhood of $140,000.
In addition, the farmer will maintain between 35 and 45 cows, each costing $1,000. The possible investment for that item could be $40,000. He will need machinery, if he can afford it, and tractors which could cost between $5,000 and $15,000. Let us take the figure of $25,000 for that item. His total machinery costs could easily be $100,000 higher. Then he will need some silos on the farm. Add $20,000 for that item.
The dairy farmer is not like another farmer who can spend between $15,000 and $25,000 for a combine which can do a lot of work. The dairy farmer needs sophisticated equipment such as milking machines and tanks, on which he could easily spend between $15,000 and $20,000. As well, he will need a milking house and other buildings, which will add another few thousand dollars to his investment. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, we are looking at an investment well in excess of $300,000.
I suggest that the government should consider allowing the dairy farmer to write off equipment quickly. The dairy farmer and his sons would be encouraged to stay in the business if they could be assured of being able to update their equipment and thus save time and labour. The question of labour is also important. I know that important advances have been made in making good labour available, but we have a long way to go. The government should also look at the farm credit situation and do what it can to help the farmer save money. I know that the ceiling on loans was raised last year to $100,000. That is an improvement over the previous situation, but I feel that the present ceiling is too low and ought to be raised to a far higher level.
